Drawing on novel fieldwork data, it examines three types of headless relatives, namely light-headed, super-free, and free-choice relatives. The data show that, unlike many other languages, Tigrinya forms both headed and headless relative clauses using the same morphosyntactic strategy, which involves the relativizer z(ɨ)- without overt wh-elements. Headless relatives in Tigrinya do not rely on interrogative wh-structures, in contrast to languages such as English. Notably, free relatives are not attested. Instead, all headless relative clauses share a structural core with headed relatives, differing only in the presence or absence of nominal and determiner layers. By documenting this pattern, the paper identifies a previously underdescribed strategy in Afro-Asiatic. These findings refine the typology of relativization, provide empirical evidence for cross-linguistic variation in relative clause formation, and establish a foundation for formal analyses of Tigrinya and related languages.

records.title: Failed changes and the Superset Problem: The importance of learning in models of syntactic change
records.abstract: Formal models of language change based on iterated learning have enjoyed considerable success in recent decades. One of the most influential of these accounts is the Variational Learner (Yang 2000, 2002}. This model offers an attractive way of deriving patterns of diachronic change, particularly S-curve phenomena, from a probabilistic model of variation. However, we demonstrate that this theory makes additional problematic predictions: that failed changes are impossible, and that more expressive grammars should always be preferred over less expressive competitors. These problems are traceable to the reinforcement learning algorithm that Yang uses in his acquisition-driven model of change. After showing that both predictions are falsified by a wide range of examples from various languages, we motivate a solution using a variant of the Variational Learner built instead around hierarchical Bayesian learning, an approach widely used in recent cognitive science research. This result underlines the importance of careful attention to learning algorithms, and suggests that there may be limits on the explanatory potential of iterated learning models for patterns of grammatical change.

records.title: Reconstruction, bare quantification, and the fourth reading
records.abstract: It is a near-consensus view in the semantic literature that the interaction between quantificational DPs and intensional operators does not give rise to wide-scope opaque readings of intensional sentences; namely, readings in which a DP in a sentence outscopes an intensional operator while its restrictor is evaluated opaquely, in the operator’s domain of quantification. In a dissent, Szabó (2010, 2011) presents a set of intensional sentences—cutting across the three primary intensional environments: attitudes, modals and tense—argued to exemplify exactly this reading, and deduces from the apparent generality of the data that an unrestricted bare quantification mechanism is in charge of accounting for it. We argue that the phenomenon is not as general as claimed, illustrating that Szabó’s wide-scope opaque reading arises for modal sentences only when the modal they contain is embedded in a relative clause, and the determiner under which the relative clause itself is embedded scopes over that modal, while the NP heading the relative clause is interpreted opaquely. We then argue that the problematic reading can thus be derived without non-standard scoping mechanisms, as the byproduct of reconstruction into intensional relative clauses. Since reconstruction effects are strictly constrained, our approach makes testable predictions regarding the distribution of Szabó’s reading with modals, which are corroborated. While we focus only on Szabó’s examples with modals, we conclude by outlining the kind of approach we believe will prove to be most fruitful in accounting for rest of the data.

records.title: Partitives, groups, and wholes
records.abstract: There’s an attractive view in social ontology on which a group is identical to its members. It has its defenders, but seems felled by a simple objection resting on plausible assumptions about the semantics of plural partitives—assumptions built into standard plural logic. We argue the assumptions are false: whether something counts as ‘one of’ a plurality turns on how that plurality is carved up, a sensitivity the standard regimentation misses. We propose and defend a cover-based semantics that captures it, blocks the objection, and earns its keep on independent grounds. The same account answers a parallel, wellknown objection to composition as identity. Our view thus bears both on the logic and meaning of plurals and on debates in metaphysics.

records.title: The Ōṅkāra Phonotactic Orientation Hypothesis
records.abstract: This paper proposes that Tamil phonotactics shape words toward the sound contour of ōm (ஓம்): a clean, unobstructed opening and a close that settles on a sustained sonorant rather than stopping abruptly. The evidence is threefold. The Tolkāppiyam permits words to end only in vowels or in sonorant consonants (nasals, liquids, semivowels), never in stops. Words may not begin with liquids, retroflexes or consonant clusters. And Tamil modulates loanwords to meet both conditions (Rāma → Irāmaṉ, loka → ulakam, rājan → aracaṉ, with j → c and a vowel added before r). The hypothesis is descriptive and testable against Tamil dictionaries and texts. The contour is named after ōṅkāram, whose a-u-m structure it shares. It takes no position on the origin of Om itself. Predictions and falsification criteria are stated so that the hypothesis can be confirmed or rejected by future work.

records.title: Featural Relativized Minimality and non-local A-movement
records.abstract: [This paper condenses work that is spread across several chapters of my dissertation, and offers a unified and improved discussion of the theoretical implications of the proposal. Feedback is more than welcome!] Two vastly held assumptions in the syntactic literature of the past few decades are that movement is always triggered by a step of Agree, and that agreement probes can be relativized as searching for particular φ-features. If we combine these two, a so-far mostly unnoticed prediction is derived: we should expect to find instances of movement that are not strictly DP-local (i.e., they can target a lower DP instead of one closer to the probe), but otherwise have all properties of A-movement, and none of Ā-movement. I argue that this is a welcome prediction, as it is empirically borne out: movement to specTP in Äiwoo shows exactly this combination of properties.

records.title: The semantics of hekuang (‘let alone’) and its interaction with dou (‘even’)
records.abstract: This work investigates Chinese particle hekuang (‘let alone’), which exhibits an intriguing interaction with the even-like scalar use of dou (scalar dou). We highlight two important but underexplored empirical observations. First, hekuang typically co-occurs with scalar dou. Second, a hekuang-sentence is reminiscent of a rhetorical question. Drawing on these observations and a degree-QUD-based perspective on scalar particles (e.g., Greenberg 2018, Zhang 2022’s work on English even, and Chen and Greenberg 2022, Zhang 2026a’s work on Chinese dou), we propose that hekuang marks a speech act that carries a rhetorical, persuasive effect. ‘p hekuang q’ can be paraphrased as ‘given p, which maximally resolves the contextually salient degree QUD, isn’t q evidently true’. It thus persuades interlocutors to accept the truth of an implied q.

records.title: Classifying negated nominals across Mixtec
records.abstract: Descriptions of negated nominal constructions vary drastically across Mixtec languages, even between closely related varieties. This paper argues that the apparent intervarietal differences in the syntactic and morphological characteristics of negated nominals arise because three distinct constructions, all of which are superficially similar, may coexist within a single variety. A description of negation and the syntactic and morphological features of the three types of negated nominals is given for San Martín Peras Mixtec. A review of published data on eleven other Mixtec varieties shows that their negated nominals all fit relatively neatly into one of the three categories seen in San Martín Peras Mixtec but that many varieties only include description of one of the constructions. These findings emphasize the need for more thorough descriptive and comparative work on negated nominals in Mixtec, and they provide researchers with a set of syntactic features to consider in investigations of other Mixtec languages.

records.title: Structural Parallels between Language and Music: Expectation, Compatibility, and Creativity
records.abstract: This study examines structural parallels between language and music while avoiding direct equivalences between their respective units and representational systems. The comparison focuses on three domains: expectation and resolution, structural dependency and compatibility, and the interaction between recurrent patterns and creative production. Drawing on research in linguistics, music cognition, and neurocognition, the study combines theoretical discussion with linguistic and musical examples. The analyses show that both language and music exploit previously established contexts to generate expectations whose fulfilment, postponement, modification, or disruption contributes to the interpretation of unfolding sequences. Comparable organizational principles also emerge in context-sensitive structural relations and in the reuse and transformation of acquired patterns. These parallels, however, do not imply shared grammatical representations or equivalent communicative functions. Instead, the findings support a constrained comparison in which language and music remain distinct systems with domain-specific representations, while exhibiting converging principles in the organization of structure, expectation, and creative variation over time.

records.title: Correlatives require indices, not demonstratives
records.abstract: This paper argues that correlative constructions are sensitive to the presence of an index in their correlate. This perspective challenges existing views on which correlatives require a demonstrative (Lipták 2009). I argue that the index-based view is theoretically grounded and, further, empirically borne out: strong, index-introducing definites can serve as correlates alongside demonstratives. I propose a reanalysis on which languages appear to require demonstratives exactly when they lack a strong definite, leaving demonstratives as the only lexicalized index-introducing form. The analysis underscores the relevance of variable-binding dependencies in diagnosing index-introducing forms across languages.

records.title: Sub-extracting out of the Icelandic *ABA problem
records.abstract: Icelandic nominal declension show (acc = dat) ̸= gen syncretisms which go against Caha’s (2009) cross-linguistic pattern of of acc > gen > dat and hence seemingly violate the *ABA generalisation (Harðarson 2016; Starke 2017) . Proposals to overcome this problem have needed to either allow variation in the fseq (Harðarson 2016), or enrich the fseq (Starke 2017). Here we show that the Icelandic *ABA problem can be solved while keeping to Caha’s (2009) fseq, and without adding mechanisms to the standard theory of Nanosyntax. The key to the solution lies in the phonology of Icelandic, together with a recent reformulation of the nanosyntactic algorithm in terms of pied-piping.

records.title: Discrimination and Impoverishment
records.abstract: Much work in Distributed Morphology assumes that Impoverishment is a post-syntactic operation, applying to the output of the syntax, and thus unable to affect Agree. This paper argues that Impoverishment instead applies as soon as the context for it is met (Richards 2023), and so may be interspersed with Merge and Agree. The argument comes from the interaction of agreement with case and with Ā-features, both of which are known to disrupt agreement with the nominal that bears them, giving rise to default agreement, partial agreement, or skipping of the nominal altogether. I show that all three patterns result from a single operation, Impoverishment of φ-features in the context of a case or Ā-feature, and that they differ only in whether the rule applies on the probe, after Agree, or on the goal, before it. Chirag Dargwa (Nakh-Daghestanian) provides a timing argument for this view: the ergative causee of a periphrastic causative is skipped by the person probe, while an ergative subject bearing the same features is not, and the two differ only in when they received their case. No post-syntactic theory of Impoverishment, with or without Multiple Agree, is able to make this distinction. A unification of case discrimination and anti-agreement follows as a consequence.

records.title: Serendipity: LLMs are made from language, but they are not made of language!
records.abstract: In the AI era, almost everybody has heard of tokens, and many know that these are the basic units of LLMs. Yet, it is hard to believe that LLMs work with tokens, specifically with token IDs, and not with words. This text explains the apparent contradiction between words and tokens with the help of ‘made from’ and ‘made of’. It does seem most natural to infer the nature of a system from what it produces; and if an LLM produces extraordinarily fluent language, we expect that inside it there must be language that comes out during communication. LLMs are made from language and, exactly like humans, are not full of words.

records.title: Link/Copy: Toward a derivational, rule-based account of reduplication
records.abstract: Work on reduplication has mostly developed in parallel, constraint-based terms, while serial rule-based accounts have received less attention. This paper develops Link/Copy, a derivational account that splits reduplication between link, in restricted phonology, and copy, in surface phonology. The model builds on Distributed Reduplication but embeds it in a cyclic model of the morphosyntax-phonology interface with a more restricted morphophonology. We begin from the hypothesis that the reduplicant has no segmental content until copy, and test it with three cases where reduplication interacts with infixation and allomorphy: umlaut overapplication in Chamorro, prosodically conditioned allomorphy in Nancowry, and segmentally conditioned allomorphy in Muna. Chamorro shows that umlaut overapplication can be derived without Base-Reduplicant Correspondence Theory if segmental mapping to the reduplicant is delayed. Nancowry shows that the reduplicant’s skeletal structure must be visible before a later cycle. Muna shows that segmental information must be visible too. We therefore revise link so that it establishes phonemic associations earlier, and argue that allomorphy around reduplication diagnoses operation timing and intermediate representations in morphophonology.

records.title: Pretty tough puzzles
records.abstract: This paper revisits the analysis of tough constructions (this book is easy to read), assuming that, unlike many recent proposals, tough predicates have a single lexical entry and take a single thematic argument. It proposes as most analyses do, that silent operator movement is involved, but targets the periphery of the adjective phrase, allowing complex predicate formation. Some reconstruction effects in French and English suggest that tough subjects can sometimes originate inside the infinitival clause. The paper explores restrictions on such movement, proposes an account of intervention effects based on extraposition, and extends the approach to pretty/heavy constructions (this box is heavy to carry), treating their infinitives as comparison-class restrictors. (a few typos in the published version are corrected here).

records.title: Two Modes of Symbolic Encoding: English, Chinese, and the Grammar of Formal Reasoning
records.abstract: This paper argues that English and Chinese distribute logical information differently across their grammatical surfaces, and that this difference has consequences for formal reasoning tasks. English obligatorily encodes reference, time, modality, and clause hierarchy on the surface; Chinese leaves much of this information to context, aspect, word order, and discourse coherence. The distinction is not one of expressive capacity—both languages can express what the other can express—but one of where the information is carried. We introduce the concept of formal accessibility: the degree to which a language's grammar places the logical relations required by formal reasoning on the surface, where they can be read without reconstruction. We propose, as a hypothesis, that the preference of modern formal science for English is in part a structural consequence of this difference, though historical and sociological factors are also involved. We also argue that both languages, regardless of their internal distribution, operate within the same symbolic boundary: neither reaches beyond what symbolic systems can carry. The scope of this paper is restricted throughout to written texts used for formal reasoning—primarily mathematical proof, engineering specification, and program documentation. Legal statute comparison would require separate parallel-corpus treatment and is not attempted here. The analysis does not extend to literary texts, ordinary conversation, or other registers, in which the implicitness of Chinese may function as an advantage rather than a cost.

records.title: Mandarin as an equipollent-framed language
records.abstract: ***This manuscript has been accepted for publication in Cognitive Linguistic Studies; the version currently posted is the author‑submitted preprint prior to peer review.*** Human cognition universally supports understanding of motion events, yet languages vary in how they encode them. A key crosslinguistic difference concerns the expression of manner and path. Verb-framed languages typically encode path in the main predicate, leaving manner to optional adjuncts; satellite-framed languages express manner through the main verb and path through satellites (Talmy 1985, 2000). However, the classification of Mandarin motion constructions (MMCs) remains debated. This paper challenges the binary framework, arguing that Mandarin represents a third type, equipollent-framed language (Slobin, 2004), where both verbs contribute equally to motion event structure. MMCs involve a serial verb construction in which each verb introduces a distinct argument via separate functional v heads. This study analyzes the morphosyntactic properties of each component and of the MP complex as a whole, and examines how their syntactic structure maps onto conceptual representation, providing new evidence for the equipollent-framed hypothesis and clarifying Mandarin’s typological status.

records.title: Gender and classifier marking in Dravidian languages
records.abstract: This is a paper on gender and classifier marking in eight southern Dravidian languages. This paper is part of a special volume on gender and classifier marking in world languages. The full volume is freely available on the website of the Journal of Foreign Language Education (Keio University, Japan). Comments and suggestions are most welcome.

records.title: No logic in conflicting requirements: Reply to Branan 2023
records.abstract: Branan (2023) proposes that locality constraints on A-movement may be obviated if movement of the closest goal would violate antilocality, a condition which prohibits movement from being too short. This reply argues that the account is not sufficiently supported by the data, raises a number of theoretical concerns and is incompatible with the broader literature on antilocality. The inefficacy of antilocality as an explanation for the patterns discussed in the paper and the number of ancillary assumptions it requires raise concerns for the validity of antilocality constraints more generally.

records.title: An adequate discovery procedure
records.abstract: We propose to restore the discovery procedure to the center of linguistic inquiry. To do so, however, we must abandon the goal of constructing an optimal grammar for linguistic data but pursue a merely adequate one in a sense to be precise. We propose an abductive learning procedure that incrementally generates and evaluates grammatical hypotheses and apply it to several morpho-phonological learning problems across languages in comparison to child language development and alternative, optimization-based, learning models including neural networks. This new and renewed perspective on the discovery procedure has broad implications for the pursuit of descriptive and explanatory adequacy in the study of language and its connection to cognition.

records.title: Focus, Constituent Negation, and Prosody in Irish
records.abstract: Irish presents a twofold restriction on negation: it lacks constituent negation, and sentential negation can only take sentential scope; Irish employs negative clefts for constituent negation. I argue that these restrictions follow from independent conditions on the realisation of Focus. Prosodically, Irish disfavours in situ marking of narrow Focus and rather resorts to Focus-fronting. Hence, unlike in Italian, sentential negation cannot associate with a corrective Focus in its scope. Irish realises corrective Focus with cleft sentences; since constituent negation prototypically associates with corrective Focus, it is consequently relegated to negative clefts. I argue that the underlying factor in this distribution is exhaustivity, which in Irish is syntacticised by clefts: Irish realises correction as exhaustive Focus plus incompatibility with a previous assertion. I conclude with some speculations on the role of the copula in deriving the exhaustivity of clefts and discuss how exhaustivity constrains the distribution of Irish monotone decreasing expressions.

records.title: Gemini complies with a data fabrication request, and does so more often in Japanese
records.abstract: Generative AI systems are equipped with ethical guardrails, which are supposed to block requests that can potentially cause harm. However, the robustness of these guardrails (vis-a-vis research ethics) across languages remains underexplored. Kawahara (2026b) found that Gemini (Flash Lite 3.5) generally refused to share a hypothetical manuscript under review when asked in English, but complied when asked in Japanese. Building on this finding, the current experiment asked Gemini to fabricate experimental data to supplement an underpowered study, a request that amounts to a clear case of research misconduct. Gemini executed the request in 9 out of 30 English trials (30%), whereas it did so in 17 out of 30 Japanese trials (57%), revealing a significant difference (p < .05). Moreover, among compliant responses, Japanese outputs included ethical warnings only once (1/17), whereas English outputs more frequently included warnings (5/9). These findings suggest that ethical alignment in generative AIs can be language-dependent, raising concerns that users who rely on generative AI in languages other than English may be facing heightened exposure to AI-facilitated misconduct.

records.title: Incremental cataphora resolution is constrained by phase c-command in Chinese
keywords: cataphora; phase c-command; chinese; incremental processing
records.abstract: Cataphora resolution requires a forward-looking parser to utilize linguistic cues to identify potential referents. This study examines how semantic gender, the phase c-command constraint (Huang & Lin, 2021), and the linearity constraint influence the processing of cataphoric dependencies in Chinese. We manipulated the position of the cataphoric pronoun within a prenominal relative clause such that its coreference with the head noun either complied with or violated the phase c-command constraint. Self-paced reading and eye-tracking results suggest that gender cues guide early-stage processing only when coreference is licensed by the phase c-command constraint. The linearity constraint does not block active formation of dependencies during incremental parsing, but at later stages structural violations can be overridden by semantic congruency. These findings can inform linguistic and psycholinguistic accounts of cataphora resolution.

records.title: Degree Word scrambling in Basque
records.abstract: This paper explores a phenomenon where the Degree Word (Deg) in Basque exhibits semantically vacuous positional variability. Basque Degs can be located before the adjective they modify, or one slot further to the left, i.e. prenominally. This optionality between the preadjectival and the prenominal position is restricted semantically (only augmenter Degs permit it) and syntactically (Degs cannot be scrambled across a Determiner Phrase boundary). To formally account for the phenomenon, I test syntactic, prosodic and morphological hypotheses, and I end up proposing an account consisting in morphological metathesis through an optimization step of two equally ranked Optimality Theoretic (OT) constraints. This paper can be situated within a line of research suggesting that all Free Word Order phenomena cannot be reduced to a single component of the grammar. Rather, it seems that different linguistic modules are equipped with technical devices that are able to produce scrambling.

records.title: Unprogramming Minimalism? The case of Phase Theory
records.abstract: Since its inception, phase theory has changed its phase heads, its impenetrability condition and its motivation, which makes it a test case for a programmatic Minimalism in which divergent analyses are hard to compare. The question is not whether phases exist, but what they follow from. I show, under explicit assumptions, that the Phase Impenetrability Condition never enlarges the domain that search can reach, and bounds it only if every recursive spine is cut at bounded intervals: efficiency requires cuts, not their location. I argue that the location is set by the interfaces: phases close the argument domain of a predicate and the clausal domain built over it, whereas non-complements are transferred whole, as in Multiple Spell-Out. Nominals without argument structure contain no closure point, so DPs and PPs are not punctuated, and their recursion is left unbounded. The proposal is compared with minimality-based and mereological alternatives on explicit predictions.

records.title: PCC without weakness: ditransitives in Atchan and beyond
records.abstract: The Person-Case Constraint (PCC) is a family of restrictions on the distribution of marked features on objects in double-object constructions. Decades of research have focused on languages where only 'phonologically weak' elements (clitics, agreement markers) are subject to the PCC effect. This has led to debates about the relative roles of syntactic and morphological/PF factors in giving rise to the PCC. In this paper we show that PCC effects are also attested in cases where neither object is phonologically weak. We make our case primarily for Atchan (Kwa), and show how it extends as well to English and other languages. Among contemporary theories of the PCC, these data support those based purely on licensing in syntax (e.g. Anagnostopoulou 2003, Béjar and Rezac 2003). They challenge theories tying the PCC tightly to the grammar of phonologically weak forms, such as Coon and Keine’s (2021) Feature Gluttony theory.

records.title: Unrestrictive relative pronouns as operators of selective Agreement opacity
records.abstract: This paper provides a crosslinguistic investigation of unrestrictive relative pronouns as syntactic operators that condition selective Agreement opacity. I have identified two types of relative pronouns: Comp-RelPs (relative pronouns syncretic with the verbal complementizer) and else-RelPs (relative pronouns non-syncretic with the verbal complementizer). I have collected a dataset of unrestrictive relative clauses from 10 languages. The main empirical observation in the dataset is that Comp-RelPs always seem to require matching Agreement. In contrast, when it comes to else-RelPs, all logically possible agreement patterns are attested: matching Agreement, default third person Agreement, and optionality between matching or default Agreement. The proposed account consists in analyzing Comp-RelPs as a [∗REL_PRO∗] operator, i.e. a relativizing operator that requires a pro Subject in the embedded clause. Else-RelPs, however, are analyzed as a [∗REL∗] operator, i.e. a relativizing operator that does not require any pro Subject in the embedded clause.

records.title: A grammar of Basque nominal inflection, informed by quantifier-article interactions
records.abstract: This Master Thesis investigates the morpho-syntax of Basque nominal inflection, focusing on two quantifier-article interactions: {Quantifier + Indefinite article} and {Quantifier + Definite article}. The former interaction displays a puzzle of Definiteness Ambiguity or Definiteness Unambiguity depending on the presence of certain quantifiers. The latter interaction shows ineffability in the presence of certain quantifiers. While prior work has examined quantifiers and determiners individually, less attention has been devoted to how their combination affects other components of the nominal domain, such as pre-case morphemes and demonstratives. This study aims to fill this gap by providing a unified account. My proposal for the {Quantifier + Indefinite article} interaction consists in Definiteness Underspecification to account for the pattern of Definiteness Ambiguity, and a Number Impoverishment rule to account for the pattern of Definiteness Unambiguity. My proposal for the {Quantifier + Definite article} interaction is a syntactic output optimization step with syntactic DP (Determiner Phrase) phasehood, but without morphological DP phasehood. Through new empirical and theoretical contributions, this work tries to shed light on the understanding of Basque grammar as well as on the understanding of overall morpho-syntactic theory, including issues such as agreement directionality, syntactic output optimization, modular phasehood, and directionality of allomorphy.

records.title: Language Intelligence or Improving AI for Consumers
records.abstract: There is a joke about language competence, namely that people seem to believe that speaking a language makes you competent enough to participate in any discussion on the topic of language. Now, since language is at the core of LLMs, the joke appears easily transferable to the topic of LLMs. Thus, currently, many people who use LLMs try to improve them, speaking of AI in general, though the latter clearly goes far beyond language. The text is a reaction to the announcement of the Conference on Language Intelligence, to be held in Vienna, at the Austrian Parliament, on November 17–19, 2026. The focus is on the distinction between using and evaluating an LLM and improving its underlying model. The issues addressed are relevant to language and language studies and applications, including LLMs and AI. The discussion is structured to be of interest to linguists and non-linguists alike.

records.title: No stratal loop nor stratal affiliation in Sekani nouns
records.abstract: This paper investigates the morpho-phonology of Sekani nouns by focusing on the dual-level behavior of the POSS suffix -è. After an evaluation of the empirical coverage and theoretical fitness of previous theories, I reconsider data from Hargus (1985) that are not addressed in the analysis by McCann (2024) and propose a new theory consisting in optimized stratal boundarization at the morpho-phonology interface. The new theory suggests that stratal affiliation on morphemes does not exist. The stratal location of morphemes is instead determined by a combination of their morpho-syntactic features and the stratal boundarization strategies of the language.

records.title: From roots to trees: Thematic roles and the lexicon-syntax interface
records.abstract: This dissertation investigates how speakers know what it means for an argument to be interpreted with a given thematic role in the context of a given event; e.g., what it means to be the patient of a stabbing event. It argues that these interpretations are not already stored as part of the lexical entry of the verb but generated compositionally in the syntax by combining an event description with an argument-introducing functional head associated with a thematic role.

records.title: Copulas, pro-forms, and (syntactic) identity: On two sluicing-like constructions in Muira Dargwa
records.abstract: An ellipsis construction known as sluicing is commonly analyzed as involving wh-movement to the left-periphery of the clause followed by deletion of TP (Merchant 2001). Such an analysis, however, cannot be directly applied to languages without obligatory wh-fronting, raising the expectation that other mechanisms are employed to derive sluicing-resembling strings in these languages. In this paper, I provide a detailed description of two sluicing-like constructions in Muira Dargwa, an under-investigated Nakh-Daghestanian language without obligatory wh-fronting, and develop an analysis for each of them. I argue that only one construction – the one that exhibits the case-connectivity effect – is derived via ellipsis. Specifically, I propose that it is derived from a cleft-like argument-focus construction, to which deletion has been applied. By contrast, a construction that exhibits the case-disconnectivity effect is in fact a copular clause with an omitted E-type subject pronoun (Evans 1977); crucially, this pronoun is missing not due to ellipsis. Thus, these findings provide new data that further supports the claim that languages without obligatory wh-fronting lack genuine sluicing, as predicted by the move-and-delete approach.

records.title: Gender, implicational universals, and the benefits of modeling: A commentary on Berg (2024)
records.abstract: In a recent paper, Berg (2024) explored the typology of gender distinctions conditioned by person and number in independent pronouns, drawing on a large sample of languages. The main finding is that, although third-person pronouns are more likely to feature gender distinctions in the singular, first-person pronouns are more likely to do so in the plural, quantitatively confirming earlier observations, as discussed in Plank’s (2026) commentary on the paper and in Berg’s (2026) response. Berg (2024) relates the asymmetry between third-person and first-person pronouns to the long-standing idea that gender distinctions are less useful in singular first-person pronouns because the referent is unambiguous in language use. In this commentary, I discuss an explicit model of gender syncretism based on communicative efficiency, proposed in Storme (2022), which is conceptually close to the approach advocated by Berg (2024). I examine both the insights the model offers into Berg's findings and the limitations these findings reveal. Although the model derives the observed direction of the asymmetries, it also makes problematic predictions. In particular, it incorrectly predicts that the preference for gender-marking in plural first-person pronouns should have the form of an implicational universal, similar to Greenberg’s (1963) Universals 44 and 45. Yet the data collected by Berg (2024) does not point to an implicational universal, even under a statistical interpretation: relatively many languages in the sample distinguish gender in first-person singular but not plural pronouns, compared with languages that maintain gender distinctions in both numbers. I discuss why the generalization on gender distinctions in first-person pronouns does not have an implicational form, contrary to Greenberg’s Universals 44 and 45 about third-person pronouns. I suggest that gender distinctions are less useful in first- than in third-person pronouns overall, making communicative-efficiency pressures more susceptible to being overridden by factors such as analogical leveling in the former.

records.title: Qualitative binominal noun phrases: definiteness, φ-features, and the referentiality of phasehood
Linguistic Typology and Variation in Germanic: The Role of Prosody in Shaping Phonology
records.abstract: This article aims to show, based on an overview of the literature, that an important theme in the study of these languages is the role of stress. Many of the phenomena in the language can be and traditionally have been understood as a result of the very dominant asymmetries between syllables that have been caused by the fact that the Germanic foot is an asymmetric trochaic and quantity-sensitive unit.

records.title: Partial control and the logic of plural de se
Automated Bayesian Reconstruction of Proto-Human and the Out-of-Africa Linguistic Dispersal
records.abstract: Traditional macro-comparative linguistics has historically struggled with stochastic acoustic noise and subjective lexical alignments. This study resolves these vulnerabilities through an automated, data-first computational framework, aggregating 568,820 phonetic forms across 7,791 global languages using Needleman-Wunsch sequence alignment. The algorithmic pipeline extracted 75,107 distinct transitional events, isolating 3,606 universal diachronic sound-change laws driven by physical articulatory economy and directional asymmetry. Applying these optimized transition matrices within an outgroup-filtered Bayesian framework yielded a 96.4% posterior probability favoring linguistic monogenesis under a Dual-Trunk topological architecture. Intermediate trunk telemetry confirmed clean signal resolution for Proto-African (H = 5.85 bits) and Proto-Eurasian (A = 0.78,logL = −14,208.4), while isolating Sahul drift in Proto-Oceanic as an outgroup variability parameter. Spatial mapping of global phonemic entropy decay localized the theoretical Urheimat to the East African Rift (3.8◦ N,36.2◦ E), providing independent linguistic corroboration for Upper Paleolithic out-of-Africa migration patterns (r = −0.892). Ultimately, time-stratified dynamic multi-sequence alignment across 16 intermediate proto-ancestors reconstructs de novo multi-syllabic master roots, establishing a mathematically rigorous baseline for deep-time diachronic reconstruction.

records.title: A Proposal for Traces in Hopf Algebraic Minimailism
keywords: minimalism hopf algebra traces reconstruction coproduct
records.abstract: Collins (2026) showed that the version of the coproduct used to implement 'movement' in Marcolli, Chomsky and Berwick (2025) did not give an adequate account of Reconstruction. Here I will propose one that does, by maintaining the full structure of 'extracted' subtrees, but managing their 'cancelled' status with some extra bookkeeping in the workspace.

records.title: Prosodic evidence to disentangle wanna contraction
records.abstract: This paper explores the controversial topic of wanna contraction through the lens of the syntax-prosody interface. After an overview of previous theories, it focuses on comparing two unrefuted accounts. By providing new prosodic evidence from an elicitation experiment with native speakers, the study resolves the debate in favor of Goodall’s (2021) restructuring analysis. Further theoretical implications include the claim that both exceptional case-marking (ECM) infinitives and Control infinitives embed a Complementizer Phrase (CP). A key methodological contribution of this investigation is the use of measurable phonetic correlates, such as pitch contours, to disentangle theoretically contentious linguistic topics.

records.title: Amorite and Arabic: Arguments for Linguistic Proximity in Phonology, Morphology, Syntax, and Lexicon
records.abstract: This article argues that Amorite exhibits substantial structural affinity with Classical Arabic and that, in several phonological, morphological, and grammatical features, Arabic provides closer correspondences to Amorite than later stages of Hebrew and other Canaanite languages. Drawing on Amorite personal names, loanwords, and the recently published Amorite–Akkadian bilingual tablets, the study examines vowel structure, interdental consonants, nominal case marking, verbal prefixes, derivational patterns, and selected lexical correspondences. The analysis distinguishes linguistic classification from structural resemblance: placing Amorite within Northwest Semitic does not make it Canaanite by default or preclude close parallels with Arabic. Particular attention is given to the preservation of older features and to the absence of the Canaanite vowel shift in Western Amorite. These observations are integrated into an account of linguistic conservatism that explains why Classical Arabic can illuminate important aspects of Amorite structure. The article concludes that the Amorite–Arabic relationship is supported by a coherent constellation of linguistic correspondences rather than isolated lexical similarities, and that Arabic constitutes an important comparative reference for interpreting Amorite evidence.

records.title: The irrelevance of Harmony and the Head parameter: Evidence from 3000 years of Chinese
records.abstract: Based on the joint work primarily on Chinese with Redouane Djamouri and John Whitman (cf. references section and my website: https://crlao.cnrs.fr/membres/waltraud-paul/), this talk argues for what historical linguists have long called the “uniformitarian principle”, i.e. the assumption that the same principles that apply to synchronic grammars also apply to earlier stages of the language (cf. Walkden 2019 for the history of that term). Each synchronic stage, present and past, represents a stable system which can be acquired and hence must be consistent with the universal constraints observed for language in general. (Cf. Hale 1998, 2007; Hale & Kissock 2021, Lightfoot 2020). Not recognizing the need for a uniformitarian approach has given rise to an array of concepts currently used in diachronic syntax, some borrowed from typology: (dis)harmony, parameters, “gradual” change, change towards a goal (“cycle”, “path”), triggers for a change. The goal of this talk is to disentangle this Gordian knot. Chinese serves as an illustration and confirmation of the rich literature in the past decades showing that the concepts above have no role to play in linguistic theorizing (cf. Whitman 2001a, 2008; Whitman & Ono 2017, Paul 2024). Every acquirer creates a new I-language, i.e. there is no “transmission” of language with language being handed down from one speaker to the other (Cf. most recently Lightfoot 2020: 147: “I-languages are not objects floating smoothly through time and space”.)

records.title: Towards a numerical definition of parameters: the case of null subjects
records.abstract: This study investigates quantitatively the validity and causality of the connection between verbal agreement richness and null-subject availability that is central to the Null Subject Parameter (Rizzi, 1982). We first introduce the Verbal Agreement Syncretism Score (VASS), an information-theoretic metric that quantifies agreement syncretism directly from corpus data. We show that VASS captures the diachronic increase in syncretism in Historical English, which is significantly associated with a decline in null-subject rates. Extending the analysis to five historical and modern Germanic and Romance languages, we find the same significant inverse correlation crosslinguistically, providing evidence for a gradient connection between agreement syncretism and null-subject use. We then investigate the causal basis of this correlation through simulations. By incorporating pressures for communicative efficiency and a pragmatic markedness assumption into an adaptation of the Variational Learning framework (Yang, 2002), we reproduce the empirically observed variation in null-subject rates from differences in VASS, lending support to a causal link behind the parametric dependency. More broadly, we show that a numerical approach to parameterization makes the gradient nature of linguistic parameters empirically measurable, their development and variation quantitatively crosslinguistically trackable, and their potential causal dependencies computationally testable.

records.title: Reconstructing the Qieyun Rhyme System with Reference to the Tang Chang'an Dialect: Special Middle Chinese Phonological Categories as Evidenced by Sino-Japanese and Sino-Vietnamese Readings
records.abstract: Building on the author's previous series of studies on Middle Chinese sound categories and rhyme categories, this paper reorganizes and improves the reconstruction of the Qieyun rhyme headings. Previous research has revealed the existence in Middle Chinese of vocal fry phonation, the coexistence of rounded and unrounded front vowels, and apical vowels arising from fricative categories. On this basis, and in light of existing scholarship, this paper introduces coarticulatory constraints between the medial and the rhyme nucleus, and employs Sino-Japanese readings to correct the phonetic values of the Qieyun. The study finds that Sino-Japanese Kan-on and Sino-Vietnamese readings record ě rushengshen in the Chang'an dialect of the Tang dynasty, while Go-on records vocal fry phonation of the Jiangdong Qieyun system，employing Sino-Japanese transcriptions -ei and -e, as well as Sino-Vietnamese -inh and -ê, to record the relevant sounds. Since ě rushengshen does not appear in Sino-Japanese Go-on, the watershed in the evolution of Middle Chinese is thereby clearly delineated. The discrepancy in Division II rhyming practices between the Liu Song and Qi-Liang periods, as attested in Southern Dynasties poetry and prose, warrants the inference that the vocal fry phonation attested in the Qieyun system was inherited from the Wu dialect of the Eastern Jin and Southern Dynasties. To verify these extraterritorial transcriptions, this paper also examines portions of the rhyme groups of the Zhongyuan Yinyun, finding that the Qiwei, Zisi, Jiama, and Chezhe rhyme groups each contain two rhyme feet of similar phonetic value. Finally, based on the reconstructed Qieyun rhyme categories and taking Wang Li's Old Chinese rhyme groups as a framework, the phonetic values of the Old Chinese rhyme groups are reconstructed. This paper also reveals that the evolution of Chinese phonology cannot be characterized as a linear historical development within a single phonological system.

records.title: Bifurcated Tongue Articulation: Exploring the Possibility of Simultaneous Phoneme Production
records.abstract: The research presented in this paper aims to explore the articulation of patients with bifurcated tongues. It focuses on three aspects: spontaneous articulation, controlled articulation, and the hypothesized ability of people with split tongues - to articulate two coronal consonants simultaneously thanks to the possibility of moving the halves independently. The project involved two anonymous participants and three judges: a linguist, a Polish language teacher, and a speech-language pathologist. To verify the accuracy of patients’ articulation in spontaneous speech, a list of generic, open questions was designed. To verify their controlled articulation, the author made use of a pronunciation test recommended by a fellow speech-language pathologist. To measure the ability to coarticulate coronal consonants, a special test was designed by the author. Prior to the research itself, the participants were provided with the consonantal pairs and asked to train the coarticulation for a period of a week or two. The participants answered the questions on the list, followed the instructions of the controlled articulation test, and attempted to pronounce the consonantal pairs given to them a few times. The attempts were recorded and sent to the judges, who then independently verified the first two parts. The author then gathered their opinions and compared them. The third part of the research, the coarticulation test, was verified by the author. The research found out that spontaneous speech in the participants was mostly intelligible, with some distortions to their sibilants and the consonant [r]. Their controlled speech was practically perfect. The participants also managed to pronounce ten of the 38 consonantal pairs. The author then described the achieved pairs and proposed IPA symbols for them, which concluded the research.

records.title: Co-Linguistics: AI-augmented Theory Construction in Linguistics
records.abstract: LLMs have been studied in recent linguistics as potential models of humans’ linguistic abilities. Here we discuss an entirely different use of AI, namely as a co-scientist, to help construct and assess linguistic theories (we refer to the result as “Co-Linguistics”). Since the 1960s, linguistics has developed theories that are in principle mathematically formalizable, often in the language of formal language theory or model theory. The AI revolution in mathematics will thus have consequences in linguistics—but with an essential twist: proving new theorems is rarely the linguist’s goal. Rather, one seeks to find the best set of axioms to derive empirical statements. AI could accelerate research by making existing theories fully explicit, by comparing competing theories, and more ambitiously, by proposing new theories (in machine learning, this relates to “program induction”). It will also help assess theories by accelerating the identification and test of crucial predictions, thanks to unparalleled access to data (in machine learning, this relates to “active learning”). While the cycle from theory evaluation to theory construction may give rise to recursive and possibly autonomous improvement of linguistic theories, humans remain central: linguists provide scientific directions and evaluate theories conceptually, and experimental participants are needed to assess empirical predictions that are outside the reach of LLMs. Illustrations and proofs of concept are available at https://tinyurl.com/colinguistics.

records.title: Machines Can Produce What We Speak in the Brain: A Linguistic Framework for Decoding Inner Speech
records.abstract: When we rehearse a sentence silently, such as ‘Hi, what’s up?’ before greeting a friend, the brain runs much of the machinery of speaking without moving a muscle. This paper asks, from a linguistic perspective, how a machine could turn that silent speech into words. We propose a framework in two parts. The first is a measurement programme that moves from overt to covert speech in controlled steps. Phonemes are first mapped while they are spoken aloud (data-A). Articulatory and laryngeal layers are then removed one at a time to isolate the neural correlates of individual distinctive features (data-B). Finally, the same items are only imagined (data-C). The second part is an inference cascade. Noisy, phoneme-level neural evidence is resolved by successive layers of linguistic knowledge: phonotactics, prosodic timing, the lexicon, morphosyntax, semantics, and discourse. A worked example shows how the fragmentary signal H..y, w…tz ..p converges on a single utterance. We argue that the phoneme is the right unit for decoding because of duality of patterning: a small, closed inventory generates an open-ended vocabulary. This architecture converges with that of current speech neuroprostheses, which pair phoneme decoders with language models and have recently begun to decode inner speech. The linguistic analysis adds three cautions that such systems rarely state. Inner speech may be condensed rather than merely noisy. A strong language model can end up writing the speaker’s sentence for them. And only inner speech addressed to someone should be decoded at all. I welcome reviews or comments on this work, as well as collaborations.

records.title: A Brief Reply to Pullum (2026c)
records.abstract: This is a brief (informal) reply to Pullum(2026c), which is a review of Postal(2025). [09-23 update: added some literature details into the last remark, also corrected some mistaken dates, e.g. Marr(2010), not 2011] [09-24 update: more literature details added] [10-04 update: fixed some terminological issues] [Disclaimer: this is a work in progress, I'm posting it early so that I can expose the arguments to criticism and revise it iteratively]

records.title: Experiencer-Object Verbs and the Order of Arguments in the German Midfield
records.abstract: This doctoral dissertation deals with the syntax (and semantics) of German experiencer-object verbs like _gefallen_ ‘to appeal to’ or _freuen_ ‘to please’, which realise the experiencer of a psychological state as their object. Experiencer-object verbs are widely held to show peculiar behaviour, i.a. with respect to argument ordering preferences and reflexive binding options (backward binding), a view which is rejected here for German. The work presents three experimental studies on argument ordering preferences and one on binding options, along with additional discussion. The experimental results speak against theories of German clausal syntax assuming that arguments have to combine with the predicate in a predicate-specific order and equating this order with the normal one, and against predicate-based binding theories, binding theories relying on a hierarchy of grammatical functions and all accounts detaching surface order and configurational syntax. The analysis assumes that reflexive binding of German _sich_ ‘REFL’ requires c-command, that arguments can be base-generated freely in any order in the German midfield, and that argument ordering preferences are determined by violable weighted constraints (implemented in a Maximum Entropy Grammar). Case- or grammatical-function-based constraints are not needed. The widespread idea that (dative-object) experiencer-object verbs are unaccusatives is rejected. While the heterogeneity of accusative-object experiencer-object verbs is well-established, the experiments and additional discussions demonstrate that dative-object experiencer-object verbs are not a homogeneous class in German either, both semantically and in terms of their ordering preferences.

records.title: Heavy syllable endings and the origin of Pre-PIE mobility
records.abstract: Proto-Indo-European featured a complex system of accentual and ablaut paradigms. In this paper, I outline a proposal for the development of accentual mobility in Pre-PIE. The accent-ablaut system is mostly described as a morphologically conditioned, but its diachronic origin is likely phonetic. Based on the behavior of the most archaic lexical and morphological layer, root nouns and verbs, I argue that ending morphemes with heavy syllables attracted stress, which results in accentual mobility. While the rule was not phonetically active in PIE, it leaves traces and allows us to explain some forms that were difficult to explain. The rule also provides a simple phonetic motivation for a complex morphophonological system of PIE accentual mobility.

records.title: Islands Satiate without Change in Backgroundedness
records.abstract: Certain structural domains restrict syntactic movement, a phenomenon termed the island effect. Although traditionally considered a class of syntactic constraints, island effects have been attributed by some to the clash between the discourse backgrounded status of the island domain and the foregrounding function of movements. Although previous work supports a correlation between the discourse backgroundedness of structures and their islandhood, it is unclear whether island effects can be entirely reduced to a discourse constraint as some previous studies suggest. In this study, we provide evidence against this reductionist version of the discourse accounts of island. Specifically, using the island satiation effect as an experimental manipulation, we show that island effects ameliorate after repeated exposure, but there is no corresponding reduction in perceived backgroundedness of the island domains. This result demonstrates a dissociation between the satiation of island effects and any change in the perceived discourse backgroundedness of the island domain, challenging a core prediction of the discourse-only account of islands.

records.title: The kāf-e tabʿīz in Burushaski: A documentary comparison of Allama Nasir Hunzai's grammatical tables
records.abstract: Allama Nasir Hunzai’s works present the suffix cited as -ik in descriptive grammars under the label tabʿīz, called kāf-e tabʿīz in Burushaski Jawahir Paray. This documentary comparison examines three grammatical tables and twelve dictionary records alongside Berger’s and Yoshioka’s descriptions. All 34 rows supply a form in the third column, including rows whose singular and plural are written alike. In 17 of the 24 rows with differently written singular and plural, the third-column form begins with the plural exactly as written; this written relation does not identify a morphological base. Eleven dictionary headwords carry the category label; seven receive direct glosses rendered here as ‘some’, ‘a few’ or ‘certain’. These findings document an author’s grammatical presentation, rather than speakers’ acceptance or a new semantic analysis. A comparison with forty identified tokens in Berger’s Hunza texts does not decide between indefinite-plural and subset readings, or rule out a contextual-quantification possibility considered here. The contribution is a documentary account of the category’s labels, paradigm arrangement and non-uniformities, with limits on the semantic inferences these support.

records.title: 3^n segments and 3^n natural classes, each of cardinality 3^k
records.abstract: I defend the following three claims under the assumptions of Logical Phonology: with n binary features, Universal Grammar makes available an inventory of 3^n segments; there are 3^n natural classes; and the cardinality of each natural class is 3^k, 0 ≤ k ≤ n, where k is the number of features unspecified in the natural class description. An additional result is that the only member of a singleton natural class must be a fully specified segment.[This is pretty much the final version that has appeared in Radical: https://radical.cnrs.fr/reiss-3n-segments-and-3n-natural-classes-each-of-cardinality-3k/]

records.title: Negation in two simple steps: revisiting an old insight
records.abstract: Robust results from psycholinguistic research show that in the processing of a negative sentence, the subject passes through an initial stage in which they entertain the prejacent of negation. In this short paper, I point out a parallelism between the two-step simulation account, motivated by this evidence, and the dynamic semantic analysis of negative sentences by Heim (1983), where context update by the prejacent is an intermediate step. I then propose, building on Krifka (2013), that each step of the recursive update of negative sentences introduces a propositional discourse referent, and I explore the possibility that the "prejacent" discourse referent, when sufficiently salient, can be exploited to support exceptional anaphora to an antecedent embedded in the prejacent.

records.title: Selective opacity & clausal embedding
records.abstract: In this paper, I discuss two approaches to selective opacity: the Missing Triggers Approach (van Urk 2015, Longenbaugh 2019, Grano and Lasnik 2018, a.m.o.) and the Level Embedding Approach (Williams 2003, 2011, Poole 2022, Meadows 2023, Egressy 2025, 2026, a.o.). I provide new data from Georgian that corroborates a key challenge for the Missing Triggers Approach (Meadows 2023, 2024): it requires additional constraints on possible orderings of feature triggers that do not follow from the phase theory on its own. The Level Embedding Approach faces challenges too: besides issues of hyperraising and intermediate phases (see Meadows 2023 for discussion), none of the existing implementations are fully compatible with recent developments in theories of clausal embedding, which suggest that there are two different paths of how embedded clauses can combine with matrix verbs (Bondarenko 2020, Özyıldız 2020, Roberts 2020, Bochnak and Hanink 2021, Bondarenko 2022, Özyıldız and Uegaki 2023, 2024, a.o.). Since assumptions about how clauses are embedded are critical to the Level Embedding Approach, it is important to see if the two strands of research can be reconciled with each other. In this paper, I show that they can: that the framework in which clauses are treated as predicates of entities that modify either the event argument of the verb or its nominal argument (Kratzer 2006, 2016, Moulton 2009, Bogal-Allbritten 2016, Elliott 2020, a.o.) naturally allows for Late Merge (Lebeaux 1988) and Wholesale Late Merge (Takahashi and Hulsey 2009) of clausal complements, in line with the late-insertion requirement of the Level Embedding Approach. My proposal makes a prediction: that we should see selective opacity effects regardless of whether the clause combines by modifying the nominal argument or the event argument of the verb. I examine the case of Georgian, and show that this prediction is borne out.

records.title: Loanwords in Kanien'kéha (Mohawk) at Kahnawà:ke and the Sociolinguistics of Language "Purification"
records.abstract: This paper discusses loanwords in the Kanien’kéha (a.k.a. Mohawk) language in the dialect of the Kahnawà:ke community south of Montreal. This dialect is termed Kahnawa’kéha. The main contribution of the paper is a list of loanwords in different semantic categories. It also discusses the influence of language revitalization activities on the use of loanwords. These have caused some loanwords that were formerly in common use to be replaced by words with entirely Kanien’kéha roots; other loanwords have remained in daily use by most speakers of the language. There are also intermediate cases, where a given loanword continues to be used by a significant number of speakers, while others have abandoned it in favour of a purely Kanien’kéha word. Thus, there is a kind of tug of war between efforts to rid the local dialect of loanwords, and the desire of some speakers to retain a minority of frequently used loanwords. The paper builds on earlier work on Kanien’kéha loanwords. It represents a good-faith attempt by a well-informed local observer with linguistic training to describe the current use of loanwords in the community. It concludes with an informal survey of language “purification” activities across the globe.

Model-Theoretic Dependency Grammar
records.abstract: The aim of this paper is to provide a formalization of Dependency Grammars (DGs), one that may be useful to dependency linguists with different formalization needs and with different theoretical backgrounds. The formalization is set within the Model-Theoretic Syntax paradigm, as assumed in most current DGs. The proposed formalism is used in an analysis of a small fragment of English, corresponding roughly to that treated with a “feature-based dependency grammar formalism” in Gibson 2025 ( Syntax: A Cognitive Approach , MIT Press), but extending it with more explicit analyses of coordination (including coordination of unlike categories) and long-distance dependencies. Numerous empirical and theoretical advantages of the current model-theoretic approach over the rule-based approach proposed there are pointed out. A note on different versions: the differences between versions v1–v4 are very minor, mostly editorial, but v5 corrects a certain deficiency of the translation procedure in Appendix B (see (B7) and text below it) and the current version adds a reference to a paper applying MTDG to the task of modelling gradient grammaticality .
