The Singulion and the Sequence: A Methodological Review of Layfield and Davis (2026a, 2026b) on the Voynich Manuscript
records.abstract: In two recent companion papers, Layfield and Davis apply latent semantic analysis (LSA) to the Voynich Manuscript and derive two hypotheses: that the manuscript was conceived as a sequence of single-bifolium quires (“singulions”) later bound out of order, and that the intended sequence of bifolia can be recovered by maximizing textual similarity across page transitions. This review examines both hypotheses against the papers’ own published data. The empirical core of the first hypothesis, an elevated textual similarity within physical bifolia, is real and independently confirmed. The reading-order interpretation built upon it, however, is not supported by the data and contradicted by the authors’ own explanation of the herbal section. The reported differential is moreover inflated by an uncontrolled variable: conjoint pages always share a Currier language, while facing pages in mixed quires can cross the A/B boundary, so part of the differential reflects language contrast rather than binding structure. The second hypothesis rests on the premise that the intended order of a meaningful text maximizes lexical similarity between adjacent pages. This premise is refuted by the authors’ own calibration manuscripts, and the resequencing experiment lacks two controls that would make its reported improvements interpretable: a permutation null distribution and a calibration on deliberately shuffled known text. A similarity-based resequencing of the manuscript is nevertheless methodologically sound under one specific model of the text, namely that page-to-page similarity reflects proximity of production rather than continuity of meaning. Three concrete experiments, each executable with the authors’ existing pipeline, would discriminate between the competing interpretations.

records.title: Meaning after the Multimodal Revolution:  Seven Things Signs and Gestures Teach Us about Meaning
records.abstract: Following a "multimodal revolution" in the language sciences, meaning is now studied not just in speech but also in sign languages ("sign") and in gestures. Seven lessons can be drawn from recent semantic research. (1) Sometimes sign makes visible key logical elements that are covert in speech. (2) Sign combines the same meaning operations as speech with a richer depictive component. (3) Sign combines the same kind of syntax as speech with a dedicated syntax for its depictive elements. (4) Even the purely depictive component of sign is linguistically structured. (5) Gestures that replace words share some non-trivial properties with signs—but unlike signs, they are not words. (6) Gestures that accompany predicates usually make backgrounded (non-assertive) contributions. (7) Several of these properties apply beyond signs and gestures, suggesting that they have a deeper cognitive source, not a narrowly linguistic one. These lessons show that human meaning results from both discrete, logical-like and gradient, iconic components, integrated through powerful cognitive mechanisms across sign, speech and gestures.

records.title: Perspective and the Self in Natural Language: the Grammar of De Se
records.abstract: This book investigates the encoding of perspective in natural language, by looking specifically at the class of attitude report known as de se reports. In a de se report, the attitude holder entertains a thought about herself from a first personal perspective. So in a typical context, ‘Ali believes that she wrote an interesting article’ reports that Ali has the thought, “I wrote an interesting article”. Exactly how this perspective on the self is integrated into the truth conditions of de se reports is a matter of long-standing debate. The book approaches this question in two parts. First, I argue that de se construal is mediated by a dedicated grammatical mechanism established at LF, known as ‘de se binding’. Evidence for this is drawn from a detailed study of counterfactual attitudes such as imagine, marshalling data from a variety of languages. Next, I show that the classical rendition of de se binding suffers from a number of problems. I develop a new semantics for de se that maintains de se binding, but which overcomes the challenges faced by previous approaches. The resulting picture serves as an affirmation of ‘de se exceptionalism’ – the view that there is something distinctive about attitudes about the self as a mental phenomenon, and that this distinctiveness is apparent in how such attitudes are encoded in the grammar.

records.title: Size- and Position-dependent opacity in Hungarian
records.abstract: Selective opacity emerges when a syntactic constituent is transparent only to certain operations. The Williams Cycle (Williams, 2003) derives opacity from structural size: Larger clauses are opaque to more syntactic operations than smaller clauses. Firstly, this paper demonstrates that Hungarian exhibits Williams Cycle effects extensively. Secondly, I bring novel data to show that the opacity of Hungarian embedded clauses depends on their final position in the matrix clause: Clauses ending up higher are opaque to more operations. Finally, I provide a unified analysis for size- and position dependent opacity by introducing a new constraint on the locality of movement. According to this constraint, movement steps must proceed along well-formed f(unctional)seq(uence)-fragments. In the absence of successive cyclic movement in Hungarian, cross-clausal movement is pre-conditioned by the re-merger of embedded clauses: If an embedded clause re-merges with an equal-sized matrix projection, the sequence of embedded heads is c-commanded by a sequence of matrix heads in a way that their union is a well-formed fseq-fragment. Consequently, sub-extraction can proceed to the matrix specifiers c-commanding the re-merger site. This derives size dependent opacity because larger clauses re-merge later, i.e. their re-merger site is c-commanded by fewer matrix specifiers. Position-dependent opacity follows because re-merged embedded clauses cannot leave their adjunction-sites, i.e. embedded clauses become transparent at the cost of their mobility.

records.title: Inclusive gender in Spanish. Subverting the heteronormative taxonomy by expressive means
records.abstract: This paper discusses the linguistic implications of the inclusive gender strategy in Spanish from a morphosemantic point of view. It is argued that inclusive gender consists of a peculiar manipulation of rules of grammar (Corver 2016). Specifically, the adding of the inclusive exponent -e in pronouns and human nouns signals the presence of a new mixed expressive morpheme in the language (McCready 2010). The truth-conditional value of -e is modeled as a partial identity function introducing the presupposition that the entity is human, whereas the expressive value gives us a profile of the speaker regarding their belief system with respect to the dominant binary taxonomy. Given the mixed nature of the new item, its use impacts not only on the expressive dimension of meaning but also on truth-conditions. Concretely, the new gender system gives up a version of the human-cloning rule according to which under some conditions human nouns in Spanish are semantically either female or male (Harris 1991). Thus, the strategy can be seen as an attempt to subvert the type of binary taxonomy that can be inferred from the current gender system. Second version (July 2026): Important rhetoric changes, including title.

records.title: Disjunction, plurality, and economy: Free Choice as distributivity over alternatives
records.abstract: Collective predication, part quantification by items like ‘both’ and ‘each’, and homogeneity provide evidence that conjunctions denote complex objects (Link, 1983; Schwarzschild, 1994; Križ, 2015). The starting point of this squib is that all of these three phenomena have counterparts with disjunction: collective predication and floating quantifiers (see also Schmitt, 2026, on similar data in German): “Heads or tails are equally likely”; “A or B both could win the race”; but also homogeneity under existential modals, the classic profile of Free Choice disjunctions (Goldstein, 2019). I also observe that the parallel goes as far as encompassing homogeneity removal: adding floating ‘each’ or ‘both’ to a Free Choice disjunction preserves its positive entailments, but under wide scope negation gives rise to a “not each”/“not both” meaning, rather than the “none”/“neither”, double prohibition profile familiar from disjunctions under negated possibility modals. On these grounds, I argue that Free Choice amounts to homogeneous distributivity over sets of alternatives. The availability of this operation, like that of other operations of closure over alternatives, is constrained by an economy principle: it is blocked whenever the same (positive) truth conditions can be achieved by replacing ‘or’ with sum-forming ‘and’ and deleting the alternative-level distributive operator in the local domain of comparison, the smallest node at which the alternative argument of this operation is saturated. This can be seen as an instance of Meyer’s (2013; 2014; 2015) more general Efficiency requirement that an LF have no simpler equivalent competitor. The constraint I propose predicts alternative-level distributivity to be allowed in sentences with possibility modals, but not in sentences with necessity modals or with non-modal predicates. Crucially, the distribution of floating ‘each’ and ‘both’ tracks that of covert distributivity over alternatives, making visible the restriction that the economy principle imposes on it: ‘each’ and ‘both’, too, are licensed in sentences with possibility modals, but not in sentences with necessity modals or non-modal predicates (and Schmitt, 2026, reports similar data for ‘jeweils’ in German). While floating part quantifiers have the same licensing conditions as distributivity over alternatives, they are also correctly predicted to affect the global truth conditions: as is familiar from the literature on homogeneity they “flatten” the truth conditions of an otherwise trivalent sentence (Schwarzschild, 1994; Löbner, 2000; Križ, 2015). Besides alternative-level distributivity and overt ‘each’ and ‘both’, this constraint also regulates existential closure but systematically leaves it available, since, as I show, the corresponding conjunctive competitor systematically isn’t equivalent to it. Distributivity over alternatives, where licensed, and existential closure together derive the range of readings associated with disjunction in non-modal sentences as well as with possibility and necessity modals, including their interaction with negation.

records.title: MLFD-5: A Multilingual Dataset of Lexical, Syntactic, and Semantic Features from Wikipedia in Five Languages
records.abstract: We present MLFD-5, a multilingual dataset of lexical, syntactic, and semantic features extracted from 1,860 Wikipedia articles in English, Chinese, Spanish, French, and German. Each document is annotated with lexical diversity measures (Type-Token Ratio, MTLD, Shannon entropy, and hapax ratio), syntactic measures derived from Universal Dependencies parsing, and 768-dimensional LaBSE semantic embeddings. The dataset is designed to facilitate reproducible cross-linguistic research by integrating interpretable linguistic indicators with Transformer-based semantic representations. Validation analyses demonstrate substantial linguistic structure in the dataset. PERMANOVA shows that language explains 35.8% of the variance in the feature space, whereas text length accounts for only 3.5%. A Mantel test reveals a significant correlation between lexical-syntactic and semantic distance matrices (r = 0.467, p = 0.001). Mixed-effects models further confirm robust language-specific effects after controlling for document length and sampling stage. MLFD-5 is publicly available through Zenodo and GitHub, together with all processing code and documentation. The dataset provides a reusable resource for quantitative typology, corpus linguistics, multilingual NLP, and cross-linguistic semantic analysis. 【1-b977d1】

records.title: On the inner-outer dichotomy of A-not-A questions: A minimalist-cartographic account
records.abstract: In this article, a fine-grained cartographic analysis of Mandarin A-not-A questions has been proposed to account for their interactions with various functional elements along the clausal spine: Inner A-not-A questions are sensitive to certain locality effects in Minimalist terms, whereas outer A-not-A questions are immune to the interference. It is proposed that the former combines two operations: The first step involves head movement to the head of PolP in overt syntax, which can be blocked by an intervening functional head. The second step involves LF feature movement to the Int head, which can be blocked by an intervening quantifier. By contrast, the latter resides in the left periphery, hence no modals or quantifiers are high enough to trigger blocking effects.

records.title: Lexical, Syntactic, and Semantic Distances Across Five Languages: A Reproducible Framework Integrating Python NLP and R Statistical Modeling
records.abstract: This study presents a reproducible framework for quantitative cross-linguistic comparison that integrates Python-based natural language processing and R-based statistical modeling. Using a corpus of 1,860 Wikipedia articles across five languages (English, Chinese, Spanish, French, and German), the study extracts lexical, syntactic, and semantic features from multilingual texts. Semantic representations are generated using LaBSE Transformer embeddings, while traditional linguistic indicators capture lexical diversity and syntactic complexity. PERMANOVA results indicate that language accounts for a substantial proportion of variation in the feature space, whereas text length contributes comparatively little. Pairwise distance analyses identify Chinese as a clear outlier and English and Spanish as the closest language pair. A Mantel test further reveals a significant correlation between lexical-syntactic and semantic distance matrices, suggesting that traditional linguistic measures align with modern embedding-based representations. Mixed-effects models confirm the robustness of language effects after controlling for text length and sampling stage. The proposed framework provides a scalable and reproducible approach to quantitative typology, multilingual corpus analysis, and computational linguistic research.

records.title: Causality Hierarchy and the Problem of Internalization
records.abstract: Recent years have seen a huge volume of literature devoted to the issues of linearization and externalization at the PF interface, which in turn provides an explicit and comprehensive account of the relationship between a highly universal hierarchical arrangement and equally diverse word orders. On the other hand, one may wonder where this universal hierarchy comes from, and how the interpretive domains can be syntacticized to its full potential. The issue is closely related to our understanding of how certain surface regularities such as temporal sequences and iconicity are “internalized” into human language faculty. We approach this issue of “internalization” by investigating how our perception of this world is encoded in cartographic terms. It is shown that a “loosely organized” causality hierarchy is deeply entrenched in a variety of syntactic constructions in Mandarin, where the first phase syntax has been extended to the “second phase” along the clausal spine, as dictated by the robust analyticity of Chinese.

records.title: Morphosyntax-Prosody Mismatch in Beijing Mandarin: Evidence from Retroflex Lenition
records.abstract: Whether Mandarin has phonemic stress has been a controversial topic in the field. Previous literature researches the phonetic evidence of stress in the language but to less avail because of the influence of tone. In my paper, I examine data from retroflex lenition from a phonological angle, arguing that the language is best analyzed with foot structures. I propose a prosodic hierarchy that allows level skipping and foot recursion. I then analyze the phenomenon under the Harmonic Grammar framework and propose an updated Match constraint that unifies morphosyntactic structures' prosodic parsing.

records.title: The distribution of tone affects prosodic parsing in Beijing Mandarin: Evidence from retroflex lenition
records.abstract: Stress in (Beijing) Mandarin, or the lack thereof, is a topic under much debate in the literature. Retroflex lenition, an optional phenomenon occurred in fast speech, provides insight into prosodically weak positions in the language. Neutral-tone syllables, on the other hand, have been traditionally analyzed as unstressed. My paper discusses that the neutral-tone syllables and prosodically weak positions predicted by retroflex lenition involve different levels of (un)stress, and that the distribution of neutral-tone syllables does not affect prosodic structures in the language. Detailed analysis of the interaction between neutral-tone syllables and retroflex lenition is constructed under the Harmonic Grammar framework.

records.title: Off phases: It's all relative(ized)
records.abstract: This paper argues that Phase Theory (Chomsky, 2000, 2001) can be subsumed by a theory of locality based on Relativized Minimality (Rizzi, 1990). Any phrase head can induce phase-like locality effects for a particular dependency, if it bears the relevant feature. C has no special status; while it reliably induces locality effects in A-bar dependencies, we find crosslinguistic variation in whether it induces locality for other dependencies. Phrases like TP induce locality effects for A-depdencies when they bear phi-features. Examining crosslinguistic patterns in long-distance A-dependencies, we tease apart the predictions of phase-based and minimality-based locality and show that minimality fares better.

records.title: Alternatives and Local Contexts in Disjunctions
Chinese Activity Constructions: Light Verb Syntax and Adnominalization
records.abstract: In Chinese Activity constructions, the Activity phrase, which consists of Actor and Activity (Actor NOMINALISER Activity), can appear either as the subject or object of the Activity verb, and in the latter case the subject is regularly the Actor (Actor V [Actor NOMINALISER Activity]). While the latter construction in which Actor and Activity co-occur is attested in all Chinese dialects, the former construction in which the Activity phrase is the subject of the verb is only found in northern dialects that generalise d-forms of the nominaliser, as southern dialects that use g-forms of the nominaliser prohibit the Activity nominal in subject position (Actor de/*ge Activity). Based on Huang’s (2008) influential account in which Activity phrases are argued to move to the subject position, Tang (2008; 2009; 2011) proposes that ge blocks verb movement from the embedded verb phrase in the Activity phrase to the matrix verb position. Due to the technical difficulties of Huang and Tang’s analyses, this paper proposes a new analysis in which Actor and Activity are argued to be merged in two separate positions in accordance with thematic principles (Ramchand 2008), and the microvariation between de and ge is argued to be due to different nominalisation strategies as the Activity phrase contains either a nominal or clausal complement. The microvariation between de and ge is hence explained by different selectional properties, for which empirical support is offered from the different etymologies of de and ge.

records.title: Focus is anaphoric, only is not
On the Syntax of Mirativity: Evidence from Mandarin Chinese
records.abstract: The aim of this paper is to investigate mirative construals in Mandarin Chinese, where the unexpectedness from the speaker's viewpoint is encoded by pure syntactic terms. Previous analyses focus mainly on languages with the evidential morphology (e.g., Gitksan, Tsafiki, etc), where indirect evidential markers can be used to express mirativity if the speaker directly witnessed the event. Mandarin, as a language without such morphology, expresses mirativity by employing either a sentence final particle a0 (i.e., a with the neutral tone), or sentential adverbials such as yuanlai 'turning out' and causal zenme 'how'. To provide a cartographic analysis, we distinguish MoodP from SAP, and split SAP further into two projections: the higher one (SAP1) indicates the relationship between the speaker and the addressee, while the lower one (SAP2) refers to the attitude of the speaker. We propose that declaratives and questions employ both, while miratives employ only SAP2, where the speaker's surprise is encoded. This leads to some very interesting results from the vantage point of the syntax-pragmatic interface.

records.title: Future shifting with present marking in Khalkha Mongolian
records.abstract: This paper examines a case of future temporal reference in Khalkha Mongolian (Eastern branch, Mongolic) that occurs in the absence of overt future morphology. When VPs are inflected solely with the tense morpheme -nA, either a present or future reading can arise, leading past descriptions of the language to characterize -nA as a non-past tense. However, the distribution of -nA raises questions for current semantic theories of the future: if a modal semantics is necessary for future temporal reference due to the uncertainty of future eventualities, does the tense morpheme give rise to the future-shifted readings on its own, or is a modal operator (covertly) present? I present novel empirical evidence that such a modal operator appears covertly alongside -nA, which I reclassify as a present tense due to its interactions with the Aktionsarten and aspect. While this modal is covert in affirmative sentences with -nA, I show that it is overtly realized under negation as the morpheme -kh. The availability of both present and future readings is traced to an ambiguity between two underlying structures: one that is future-oriented, and one that is present-oriented. In the future-oriented structure, future temporal reference stems from the presence of a covert modal operator and covert prospective aspect. Altogether, I argue that a modal analysis of future reference is needed, even when no modal appears on the surface.

records.title: Grammatical acceptability is affected by the fit between the construction and noun phrase/contextual meaning: Evidence from six pre-registered judgment studies
records.abstract: Human language allows for virtually limitless productivity. Why, then, are certain perfectly-comprehensible sentences (e.g., *The boy dragged the girl the box) deemed ungrammatical by native speakers? Here, we test the prediction of Construction Grammar accounts (c.f., Categorical Grammar accounts) that grammatical acceptability is probabilistically affected by the compatibility between the meaning (semantics) of the construction (e.g., [AGENT] [ACTION] [RECPIENT] [PATIENT]) and (a) the nouns (e.g., "The boy sent the girl the package" is more grammatical than "*The boy sent Chicago the package"; Studies 1,3,5) and (b) the speaker’s intended meaning in context (e.g., the team in the Chicago office > the geographic location; Studies 2,4,6). Across a series of six large (N=100) pre-registered studies, we find that (in all but one case), both of these factors significantly affect English speakers’ rated acceptability of sentences, across the transitive and periphrastic causative (e.g., "The clown made the man laugh" vs *"The clown laughed the man"); the to- and double-object dative (e.g., "The girl said something to the boy" vs "*The girl said the boy something") and the active/passive (e.g., "The book cost $10" vs "*$10 was cost by the book"). These findings constitute support for Construction Grammar approaches, under which this type of grammatical acceptability results from a probabilistic semantic clash, and against Categorical Grammar accounts, which can explain graded (as opposed to categorical) ungrammaticality only via some kind of add-on.

records.title: Modifiers or adjectivizers? A featural decomposition of the A'ingae evaluatives
records.abstract: A'ingae (ISO 639-3: con) has three evaluative morphemes (the augmentative -ʔu/-ʔ AUG, diminutive -ʔvi DMN, and ambivalent -ʔkhu AMV) which can be used either as nominal modifiers or as adjectivizers. Across the two functions, the segmental phonology of the evaluatives stays constant, but their stress assignment differs—the nominal modifiers stress the second syllable to their left, while the adjectivizers preserve underlying stress (if present), and stress the preceding syllable otherwise. To account for both their similarities and differences, I propose that the A'ingae evaluatives realize complex feature bundles. The modifiers expone [AUG, EVAL], [DMN, EVAL], [AMV, EVAL], and the adjectivizers expone [AUG, a], [DMN, a], [AMV, a]. The features [AUG], [DMN], and [AMV] shared across the two functions capture their segmental content. The function-specific features ([EVAL] and [a]) capture their distinct stress assignment patterns. Thus, the A'ingae data demonstrate that morphological exponence may involve not only segmental content, but also phonological processes (Hockett, 1954; Anderson, 1992; Sande, 2020; Sande, Jenks, and Inkelas, 2020), and that the realization of any single morpheme may stem from a non-trivial interplay of elements introduced by different features.

records.title: Anti-factive “pu” in Northern Greek dialects
records.abstract: I show that the complementizer “pu” in Northern Greek is not always restricted to factive complements and can trigger an anti-factive inference. This contrasts with Standard Modern Greek “pu”, but is in line with other Greek dialects where “pu” is a generic realis—rather than a factive—complementizer (Nicholas 1998). I show that similar inferences arise with the complementizer “pos”. I argue that the incompatibility of “pu” with the definite article is independent of factivity (contra Roussou 1992, 1994), since it persists in dialects where “pu” is not factive, and since *to pos is also ungrammatical, in addition to *to pu (Angelopoulos & Tsilia 2026). I suggest that “pu” and “pos” share a question feature, inherited from their wh-uses, which contributes speaker-side questioning of the embedded proposition. This teaches us that “pu” is not always factive, that “oti” and “pos” are not in free variation, and that the explanation of *to pu cannot be tied to factivity.

records.title: The Grammar of Defeated Expectations: the case of wh-exclamatives
records.abstract: This dissertation investigates how the grammar expresses defeated expectations through matrix and embedded wh-exclamatives, such as “Wow, how smart Maria is!” and “George is surprised at how smart Maria is”. It asks two central questions. First, why do wh-exclamatives morphosyntactically resemble wh-interrogatives cross-linguistically, while behaving differently from both interrogatives and declaratives? Second, what is the role of negation in wh-exclamatives when it appears redundant, not reversing the truth value of the sentence? I show that wh-exclamatives are not merely exclamatory uses of declaratives or interrogatives, and I disentangle the speech act of exclamation from the clause type of wh-exclamatives. I argue that the resemblance between wh-exclamatives and wh-interrogatives is not accidental: exclamatives are built from interrogatives plus “surprise” (or a predicate with an equivalent meaning). A wh-exclamative expresses the surprise of the speaker (for root exclamatives) or the attitude holder (for embedded exclamatives) at the answer to the question. I propose that the structure of root exclamatives is “wow-type particle + Q”, where “wow” a speaker-anchored “surprise/amaze/can’t believe”, and that of embedded exclamatives “surprise-type predicate + Q”. This accounts for their interrogative-like morphosyntax without reducing them to questions semantically: a question asks for an answer, whereas an exclamative expresses or describes surprise at an answer. The analysis has consequences for question embedding. Following Grimshaw (1979), I argue that embedded exclamatives must be distinguished from embedded interrogatives, and that the typology of clause-embedding predicates must therefore be expanded. Predicates such as “wonder” embed interrogatives but not exclamatives; predicates such as “surprise”, “amaze”, and “cannot believe” embed exclamatives but not genuine interrogatives; and predicates such as “know”, “tell”, and “find out” can embed both. I predict that the latter, on their exclamative use, contain a covert surprise-type predicate, and I provide several empirical arguments that support this prediction. Furthermore, I introduce a paradigm showing that declarative and question-embedding “surprise” as well as matrix exclamatives all have different discourse contributions. I argue that surprise-type predicates need to have access to their prejacent question/set of propositions, and thus that answerhood operators should not be applied to the question complement before it composes with the predicate. I also discuss the puzzling absence of polar and alternative whether-exclamatives. The second part of the dissertation turns to a cross-linguistically recurrent negation in wh-exclamatives, which I call Cover Negation (e.g., How often have I (not) watched this series! ). Examining the phenomenon cross-linguistically, I show that this negation is not expletive and has certain cross-linguistically recurring properties: it resists stress, does not license negative polarity items, permits positive polarity items, often appears with a discourse-initial “and” or “wh all”-type material, and is blocked by relative-clause complementizers. I argue that Cover Negation contributes a coverage reading: the speaker is surprised that the actual wh-values instantiate sufficiently many contextually salient categories. Formally, it performs complementation over a contextual cover, a structured set of categories in the wh-domain. I discuss other corners of the grammar where such a wh-domain is attested. The broader conclusion is that exclamatives are not peripheral expressive constructions. They illuminate how clause types are built from one another, how embedding predicates interact with questions, how language expresses or describes surprise, how negation can operate over structured alternatives, and how wh-domains are organized into contextually salient categories.

records.title: Reduplication Without Syllable Copying
records.abstract: Several theories of reduplication have attempted to accommodate the typologically rare option of syllable copying, arguably attested in Yidiɲ (mu.la-mu.la.ri ‘initiated men’, ŋa.lal-ŋa.lal ‘big ones’). We revisit the pattern, concluding that it does not support the traditional characterization. Rather, Yidiɲ reduplication targets morphological roots most of the time, and truncates roots longer than two syllables after the second vowel. The theory of reduplication best suited for this type of pattern is Serial Template Satisfaction, which we modify to allow only segmental and morphological copying. The shape of templates is mediated partly by prespecification at the UR level and partly by markedness constraints. This theory is compared with two alternatives: Base-Reduplicant Correspondence Theory (BRCT) and Morphological Doubling Theory (MDT). We argue that BRCT has difficulties with opacity in Yidiɲ reduplication, while MDT cannot characterize the basic phonological generalizations about the shape of the reduplicative affix or the bracketing paradoxes in verbal reduplication.

records.title: The long and short of subject focus in Igbo
records.abstract: Focus constructions in Igbo feature a set of subject/non-subject asymmetries. Subject focus constructions lack both the left peripheral morphology and the tonal reflex of A′-movement which are present when a non-subject is focused. I argue that these asymmetries diagnose neither a lack of left peripheral structure, nor a lack of A′-movement in subject focus clauses – focused subjects move to the CP layer. The surface differences reflect the fact that non-subjects, but not subjects, undergo successive cyclic A′-movement from the edge of the vP, and subjects, but not non-subjects, move from a position linearly adjacent to the complementizer domain. This proposal provides support for the existence of A′-movement reflexes at the vP edge, implicating a clause-medial phase, and C-trace effects at PF.

records.title: A Glance at French Pseudopassives
records.abstract: This. paper uses the technology developed in Johnson and Postal (1980) ARC PAIR GRAMMAR, to deal inter alia with facts which have totally befudled French grammarians since the 19th century. To my knowledge day, in 2026, there remains no alternate treatment to that in the listed paper.

records.title: "And" as disjunction?
records.abstract: This note makes two points concerning the prediction of Fox (2007) according to which disjunction should end up as conjunction in the absence of a conjunctive alternative. The first point is that Fox’s theory only makes this prediction when the disjuncts are not logically mutually exclusive. The second one is that, when the first point is taken together with Singh’s (2008) claim that "or" requires that its arguments be mutually exclusive, it may become possible to analyze both "and" and "or" as disjunctions with no conjunctive alternative, potentially explaining the homogeneous behavior of "and".

records.title: Palatalization in Educated Cairene Arabic
records.abstract: In the speech of some educated Cairenes, the coronal stops /t d tˤ dˤ/ acquire a secondary palatal articulation before high front vowels and glides, resulting in [tj] or [dj]. Based on first-hand data, this article provides a detailed phonetic and phonological investigation of this palatalization process in an attempt to fill a descriptive gap in the literature on Cairene Arabic. By examining the full range of triggers, targets, and potential blockers, I demonstrate that this is a phonetic coarticulatory effect, and that it should be distinguished from phonological assimilation. I also explore the hypothesis that this process – characterized as a sound change in progress – has been phonologized in a different sociolect of Cairene Arabic.

records.title: The Adjectival Relative Construction in Egyptian Arabic
records.abstract: The present paper investigates a type of broad-subject construction in Egyptian Arabic in which an adjective or participial structurally qualifies the head noun (or subject) but logically qualifies a subsequent noun, as in ir-raagil [il-ħilwiin banaat-u] 'the man the beautiful.PL his daughters'. This Adjectival Relative Construction is interesting in that it incorporates properties of both relative clauses and adjectival phrases. I evaluate the main analytical approaches in the literature and conclude that it must be analyzed as a hybrid type of nominal modifier that has adjectival and relative characteristics. Binding to the head noun is accomplished through a semantically motivated resumptive pronoun.

records.title: The phonology and micro-typology of Arabic R
records.abstract: The R sound exhibits considerable variability both across and within Arabic dialects; one that covers place and manner of articulation, as well as the notorious emphatic-plain distinction. Some R phones are in contrastive distribution, while others are contextually conditioned or free variants. This article aims to establish the underlying R phonemes in the spoken varieties of Arabic, evidence of which is sought in R’s dialect-specific phonological behavior: in minimal pair contrasts, distributional phenomena, loanword phonology, and phonological processes that target or are triggered by R. Investigation of such evidence reveals four major patterns based on the nature and number of R phonemes, consequently classifying Arabic dialects into four types: the split-R dialects (primarily Maghrebi and Egyptian dialect groups), the emphatic-R dialects (the Levantine group), the plain-R dialects (the Gulf group together with most peripheral dialects), and the uvular-R dialects (the qeltu-dialects of Mesopotamia). The analysis employs a minimalist, contrast-based model of feature geometry to characterize aspects of the attested R’s – such as emphatic-ness, coronality, dorsality, and sonority – and shows that the typology is directly mirrored in the representation. This has theoretical implications as well. Diverse rhotic representations within closely related language varieties demonstrate that distinctive features should not be interpreted as rigidly as is often assumed, and call attention to the semi-arbitrary relationship between phonetics and phonology.

records.title: Contrastive Feature Typologies of Arabic Consonant Reflexes
records.abstract: Attempts to classify spoken Arabic dialects based on distinct reflexes of consonant phonemes are known to employ a mixture of parameters, which often conflate linguistic and non-linguistic facts. This article advances an alternative, theory-informed perspective of segmental typology, one that takes phonological properties as the object of investigation. Under this approach, various classi-ficatory systems are legitimate; and we utilize a typological scheme within the framework of feature geometry. A minimalist model designed to account for segment-internal representations produces neat typologies of the Arabic consonants that vary across dialects, namely qāf, ǧīm, kāf, ḍād, interdentals, rhotic, and pharyngeals. Cognates for each of these are analyzed in a typology based on a few monovalent contrastive features. A key benefit of the proposed typologies is that the featural compositions of the various cognates give grounds for their behavior, in terms of contrasts and phonological activity, and potentially in diachronic processes as well. At a more general level, property-based typology is a promising line of research that helps us understand and categorize purely linguistic facts across languages or language varieties.

records.title: Phases, Derivational Layers, and Angles: approaches to locality
records.abstract: Classical Phase Theory suffers from a number of conceptual problems, which I sketch out here. Layered Derivation approaches (e.g. Zwart 2009, 2017) solve some, but not all of these. I suggest that rethinking the core syntactic operation, so that it is not set-theoretic Merge, but rather part-theoretic Subjoin, following Adger (2025), provides a new and improved perspective on these issues.

records.title: Social Meaning and Minimalist Syntax
records.abstract: This chapter argues that the basic architecture of minimalist syntax does not need to be expanded to be consistent with the existence of variation of the kind that is of interest to sociolinguists: the core mechanisms of Merge and Agree, together with the ways that features are assumed to enter into dependencies are sufficient to provide an elegant model of such variation. The question then is whether social meanings are to be incorporated into such a feature checking mechanism, which is clearly technically possible and has been suggested in the literature. I suggest the answer to this should be no, and advocate for a stronger position, where social meanings are interpretations of structure, rather than being part of the grammat- ical representation itself, as more in keeping with the broader goals of minimalist syntax as an autonomous system with as few primitives as possible.

records.title: Syntactic islands as symmetry breaking: Rock, paper, syntax
records.abstract: Syntactic movement and its relation to syntactic islands is a core tenet within linguistics. However, the existence of said islands affecting the grammaticality of movement presents a challenge for connecting the two while modeling syntactic movement under internal merge within the minimalist program. Most approaches modeling island effects through PIC present several flaws, presenting both theoretical inconsistencies with the minimalist program, and limited empirical coverage of linguistic data. Departing from a new mathematical model of merge that is not labelless and that includes group theory and its related symmetries, PIC together with formal properties of the minimalist program such as ciclicity and c-command are derived from it while most categorical island constraints are reduced to symmetry breaking. The relabelling proposal presented here is supported by a mathematical model that reduces the additional formal machinery of the minimalist program, an analysis of syntactic movement in small clauses, case assignment in partial indirect questions, general distribution properties of syntax and sluicing. The results under the present model of merge suggest that categorical island effects on syntactic movement emerge as a result of symmetry breaking between either the two copies, or the copies and the resulting label of the higher copy landing site.

records.title: Weak Crossover and Global Competition
records.abstract: Weak Crossover (WCO) describes the fact that movement dependencies like "which boy_1 did his_1 mother scold?" are unacceptable on the intended bound reading. Reviving and updating an old idea due to Eddy Ruys (1994), this paper proposes that WCO effects in overt-movement dependencies are a byproduct of a principle of competition between semantically equivalent structures: the WCO structure loses to an equivalent structure that involves shorter movement dependencies. I'll present a series of arguments for this theory, based on both new data as well as known facts which have thus far escaped analysis in the literature on crossover. The theory also offers a relatively simple explanation for why A-movement is immune to crossover effects.

records.title: An experimental comparison of at-issueness diagnostics
records.abstract: At-issueness is a key concept in semantics and pragmatics, distinguishing the main point of an utterance from background information. However, there is no consensus on how at-issueness should be defined or diagnosed, given that different diagnostics for at-issueness align with different definitions and rely on different assumptions about properties of at-issue content. This paper presents an experimental comparison of five diagnostics of at-issueness, applied to the contents of non-restrictive relative clauses and the complements of clause-embedding predicates. The results are mixed: While some comparisons of the results of diagnostics reveal differences, suggesting that the diagnostics are not interchangeable, other comparisons yield more consistent results. The paper develops several hypotheses about factors that may lead different diagnostics to give different results and cautions against concluding that differences between the results of two diagnostics means that they probe distinct underlying properties (cf., Snider 2017a; Koev 2018).

records.title: Semantic Conditions on Disjunctive Number Agreement [Dissertation]
records.abstract: This dissertation examines verbal number agreement with disjunctive subjects. Whereas disjunctions, like indefinites, are known to freely take existential scope above other sentential operators — even out of environments from which scope-taking is typically blocked — I show that scope readings are more limited in sentences where disjoined singular subjects control plural agreement. In particular, I argue that plural-agreeing SG-SG disjunctions must take existential scope within a polar question or beneath a downward-entailing or quantificational operator. I call this pattern Ivlieva’s Generalization based on Ivlieva (2012, 2013). While Ivlieva’s findings conflict with other existing accounts of disjunctive agreement, I present data — primarily from English, but also from Spanish, German, and Romanian — that strengthen the case that plural agreement with disjunctive subjects is semantically restricted. The cross-linguistic convergence of evidence indicates that the restricted distribution of plural disjunctive agreement owes to more general properties of disjunction and agreement rather than language-internal factors. I show that disjoined singular subjects that control singular verbal agreement, as well as disjoined plural subjects that control plural verbal agreement, display none of the same semantic restrictions. That agreement morphology correlates with semantic environment may seem surprising under a feature-copying view of agreement, but I show that the pattern becomes more familiar once we compare the distribution of plural-agreeing disjunction to that of other semantically marked indefinites, such as negative polarity items and epistemic indefinites. Though the empirical signature of each class of words is slightly different, considering plural-agreeing disjunction within the larger typology of indefinites (e.g., Haspelmath 1997) makes its distribution less anomalous. Compared to these other marked indefinites, the difference with plural-agreeing disjunction is that its distributional restrictions correlate with a reflex external to the nominal (namely, the verbal agreement) rather than with a lexical alternation within the nominal itself. I also show that the semantic environments where plural-agreeing disjunction can take existential scope strongly resemble the environments that block cross-sentential anaphora to indefinites. In light of these cross-domain connections, I present a formal account using tools from Giannakidou (1998, 2011)’s analysis of NPIs and Kamp and Reyle (1993)’s Discourse Representation Theory (DRT). In my account, the morpheme that is responsible for plural agreement with disjunction also restricts how the disjunction can existentially quantify over the disjunctive alternatives. Finally, I reconcile Ivlieva’s Generalization with past studies reporting that verbal agreement with disjoined subjects is simply unpredictable, rather than sensitive to semantic environment, as I argue it is. These previous studies primarily examine sentences where disjunction appears in matrix clauses without any overt quantification, and tend not to control for pragmatic context. I show that controlling for context allows us to better predict when singular and plural disjunctive agreement will be possible. Further, I argue that in some contexts, covert modality can provide the licensing environment that plural disjunctive agreement requires.

records.title: Semi-lexicality: the state of the art
records.abstract: This paper is a state of the art paper on the linguistic phenomenon ‘semi-lexicality’. We discuss what a semi-lexical item is, namely an item which is typically considered to be from a lexical, open class (noun, verb, adjective) but which shows morphosyntactic and/or semantic properties that are usually associated with elements from functional, closed classes (quantifiers, auxiliaries, et cetera), and its theoretical relevance for the field of generative linguistics. In the first part of the paper, we relate the notion of semi-lexicality within generative linguistics to the notions of fuzziness and gradience in the fields of cognitive and functional linguistics. In the second part, we discuss earlier and later approaches to semi-lexicality within the generative framework. In the third part, we discuss the connection between grammaticalization and semi-lexicality, with a particular focus on recent generative approaches which explicitly tie these two notions together in one formal analysis.

records.title: The syntax of verb-object phrases in Chinese: constraints and reanalysis
records.abstract: This revised version of my doctoral dissertation was published nearly four decades ago in 1988 and available on my website since 2010 (https://crlao.cnrs.fr/membres/waltraud-paul/). The reason for posting it now on lingbuzz with its much larger audience is the renewed interest by neurolinguists in the data set extensively discussed in my thesis. Here’s the background. Chinese has verb-object phrases (VOP) whose meaning can be compositional or non-compositional: bō ‘remove’ pí ‘skin’ = ‘peel’, kāi ‘open’ dāo ‘knife’ = ‘operate (on)’. Given their phrasal status, the verb can bear aspectual suffixes and the object can be modified; only the latter shows some constraints in the case of idiomatic VOPs. The patient of the VOP as a whole (i.e. the fruit to be peeled, the person to be operated on) must not follow the VOP, due to the Phrase Structure Condition, a general principle of Chinese syntax (cf. C.-T. James Huang 1982, ch. 2). Instead, it can occur in preverbal position, preceded by bǎ (still misanalysed as a preposition in Paul 1988), gěi ‘to, for’ or gēn ‘with’. The particular form for encoding the patient needs to be specified in the lexicon, both for compositional and non-compositional VOPs. Against this background, the thesis uses a fine-grained analysis of VOPs as a red thread to explore different core domains of Chinese syntax. Notwithstanding the myriad of syntactic arguments in favour of the phrasal status of VOPs, they are still often considered verbs, i.e. words (V°), which for mysterious reasons can be “separated” (e.g. by an aspectual suffix on the verb: V-Asp O), hence the label "separable verbs". These contrast with so-called "inseparable verbs", i.e. bona fide compound verbs (V°) such as chū ‘produce’- bǎn ‘printing.plate’ = ‘publish’ ([chū-(*Asp) bǎn] -Asp) . The main reason for the incorrect analysis as words (V°) seems to be the often observed non-compositionality of meaning and the (mis)assumption of an isomorphism between syntax and semantics. Neurolinguistic research now (mis) takes these so-called “separable verbs” (i.e. VO-phrases) as representative of the morphological domain and performs different experiments, inter alia with the aim to challenge the distinctness between morphology and syntax via the obtained neural responses (cf. as the most recent example Yu et al 2026 and similar studies cited there: https://doi.org/10.1111/cogs.70220). Unsurprisingly, the results are often not very conclusive and quite a lot of speculations are offered in terms of explanation. However, no-one goes back to their initial experimental design and realizes that their purported words are in fact phrases.

records.title: Pivoting away from isomorphism: Content, Sound, and Constituent Structure
records.abstract: We make the double claim that the domain of Content (‘lexical meaning’) is not a constituent, ‎but a Span, and that the search for atomic Content is contingent on phonological representations. ‎We argue for such a dependency based on properties of (so-called) Hebrew complex prepositions, ‎such as ʕal jed-ej (múzika), ‘by (music)’ (lit ‘on hands of music’). The sequence P+N(+X) in ‎Modern Hebrew (MH) as well as in Biblical Hebrew and interim periods comprises hundreds of ‎attested tokens with rich idiosyncratic Content. However, the phonological, prosodic, Content, and ‎syntactic properties of P+N(+X) combinations do not align, with N forming a constituent with its ‎complement that excludes P (jedej muzika), but with Content and phonological properties ‎associated with the non-constituent P+N (ʕal jedej) arguing for the syntactic structure [ P [ N ‎DP/X]] in which Content can be associated with the non-constituent P-N, a Span. To affirm that ‎conclusion, we discuss and dismiss on empirical grounds several alternative analyses, among ‎which (i) the view that P+N are an instance of a possibly complex P; (ii) the possibility that N ‎incorporates into P; (iii) the possibility that Content is associated not with the sequence P-N, but ‎with N alone in the context of a designated P. ‎

records.title: Prefixoids aren't prefixes: not all inseparable complex verbs are (underlyingly) the same
records.abstract: The goal of this paper is to investigate the structural distinctions that exist between prefixoids and prefixes in modern Dutch, with an empirical focus on inseparable complex verbs (ICVs). Adopting a derivational, separationist approach to the syntaxmorphology interface (Distributed Morphology), we maintain that the fundamental difference between prefixoids and prefixes is that the former are clitics while the latter are initially merged with roots lower in the first phase (vP) prior to when these complex predicates are labeled (by v). As clitics, prefixoids are adjoined to the left-edge of the first phase (with the phase head v). Our theoretical claims are further substantiated by data extracted from the Dutch Celex Lexicon, providing a detailed assessment of the categorical status of the stem that prefixoids and prefixes attach to, their ability to contribute a resultative interpretation, and their potential effects on the argument structure of the ICV.

records.title: A semantic analysis of Cantonese sin
records.abstract: In this thesis, we investigate the multifaceted uses of the Cantonese particle sin (先). Firstly, we argue with historical evidence that the temporal sin derives the question focus sin and the scalar sin separately. Secondly, we argue that the formulations of temporal sin derives question-focus by type-shifting: while temporal sin arranges the sequence of two propositions, question sin arranges the sequence of two questions. Then we argue that semantics of scalar sin gives a long presupposition between its prejacent p and a contextually salient expectation r. It combines with various exclusive particles by predicate modification. Decomposing the scalar and the exclusive components resolve the directionality puzzle: a single sin can associate with various exclusive particles, which can have either directionality.

records.title: A REPLY TO TERENCE TAO’S OPEN LETTER “A SEVERE MISALIGNMENT OF AI IN MATHEMATICS” (Reflections relevant to linguistics, too)
records.abstract: I see the concern about AI and the future of scientific fields such as pure mathematics and linguistics somewhat differently. AI opens new perspectives much more than it closes disciplines—everything is a matter of a standpoint. (This comment was submitted to Terence Tao’s moderated blog on September 22, 2026, but has not been published there yet: https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2026/09/11/a-severe-misalignment-of-ai-in-mathematics/)
