records.title: Parameters of counting: Khasi and the crosslinguistic landscape
records.abstract: This paper develops a unified analysis of cardinal expressions, challenging the assumed complementarity between number marking and numeral classifiers (Chierchia 1998; Borer 2005). Drawing on original fieldwork data from Khasi, I show that functional plural marking and individuating numeral classifiers obligatorily co-occur in counting constructions. I argue that this pattern follows once the two are assigned distinct grammatical functions: number marking encodes grammatical number, while classifiers provide the atomic structure required for counting. Building on the Nominal Mapping Parameter (Chierchia 1998), I propose that counting universally requires classifiers and derive cross-linguistic variation from two parameters. The Nominal Mapping Parameter determines noun denotation and the availability of #-based number marking, while a Card/CL Bundling Parameter (Giorgi & Pianesi 1997; Pylkkänen 2002) determines whether Card and CL are projected separately or bundled into a single complex head. Their interaction derives four attested counting systems, exemplified by Mandarin, English, Khasi, and Dëne Sųłiné. I further extend the analysis to apparent classifier optionality and mismatches between morphological and semantic plurality, suggesting that these may follow from the interaction of Economy and syntactic-semantic symmetry (Swart & Farkas 2010). The paper argues that classifiers are a universal component of cardinal composition and that number marking and numeral classification reflect independent dimensions of cross-linguistic variation.

records.title: Scaling up skills-based grading for introductory syntax
records.abstract: In an attempt to better support student learning and well-being, educators have been increasingly turning to "alternative" methods of grading. One particular approach, skills based grading, breaks down the learning outcomes into discrete "skills" that students can demonstrate directly, within a transparent grading structure. Previous success stories for skills-based grading in linguistics required a significant amount of grading data entry by hand, and were confined to small-to-medium-sized specialist classes. We report here on an implementation of skills-based grading in the syntax component of an introductory course, where the size of the class (150-180 students) and resourcing constraints required us to scale up from existing models. Our implementation included automatically-graded online exercises, short written assignments that can be graded quickly, and an optional short assignment for deeper syntactic thinking, all of which served to make syntax more approachable. We discuss a range of quantitative and qualitative findings indicating that this approach benefits students and faculty, and conclude with recommendations for colleagues who might also be interested in centering learning and feedback in their assessments.

records.title: On the relationship between privative and equipollent feature specifications
records.abstract: Equipollent and privative feature specifications are formally compared. A bijection is proven between consistent and complete equipollent and privative segments, grounding the intuition that under- and contradictory specifications have no equivalent in privative systems. However, it is shown that there exists no isomorphism between equipollent and privative natural classes, grounding the intuition that the former defines natural classes inexpressible in the latter.

records.title: Pictures and Figures: Golding, Halliday, and the Stratum Closest to Being
records.abstract: This version returns to Golding's final chapter with the full framework available and enacts the paper's convergence argument one final time: Golding calls it a password, the present paper calls it the unspeakable remainder, they are the same thing. Tuami is named as the first artist, the haft as the first artwork, carrying the figural ground briefly touched and leaving its trace in carved ivory.

records.title: The loud silence of echo
records.abstract: 'Echo questions', or 'echos' for short, ask the addressee to clarify the utterance they just produced by repeating (some part of) it. We can distinguish between polar echos (asking if their prejacent matches the antecedent utterance) and wh-echos (asking a wh-question about some part of the antecedent utterance). We can also have echos to antecedent utterances of different types. Thus, (1)-(4) illustrate polar and wh-echos in English to assertions, polar questions, wh-questions, and imperative directives. (1) a. A: I gave you a book. B: {You gave me a book? / You gave me what? / What did you give me?} (2) A: Did you give me a book? B: {Did I give you a book? / Did I give you what?} (3) A: What did you give me? B: {What did I give you? / What did I what?} (4) A: Give me a book. B: {Give you a book? / Give you what?} In English, echos tend to use non-neutral forms (e.g., rising declaratives and imperatives, wh-in-situ questions), but these forms typically still have non-echo uses, and in general, the internal structure of English echos is not always clear from their form. While it is commonly assumed that prosody can distinguish echo vs. non-echo questions, Biezma et al. (2021) claim that neither word order, nor prosody reliably distinguish echo vs. non-echo interpretations of wh-questions in English and conclude that the difference between echo and non-echo questions (of any type) is not their compositional semantic representation, but "their position in the discourse". In other languages, people have observed form differences between echo and non-echo questions that ostensibly necessitate distinct compositional representations. For instance, Sudo (2007) shows that Japanese echo vs. non-echo questions use different particles and proposes that the 'tte' particle, which only occurs in echo questions, realizes a special ECHO complementizer. In this paper, I look at morphosyntactic and prosodic properties of different types of echos in Russian. I show that while there doesn't seem to be a systematic overt way to realize any kind of ECHO operator in Russian (segmental or suprasegmental), we have evidence that echos in Russian systematically involve embedding under a silent ECHO predicate, which is a speech report predicate anaphoric to the antecedent utterance.

records.title: Phraseology and Terminology
When I am you: Deriving honorifics through weak indices
records.abstract: Honorifics across languages tend to recruit specific phi-features (e.g. plural and 3rd person) for polite reference to the addressee. Wang (2023) derives this regularity pragmatically from the interaction between Maximize Presupposition! and a Taboo of Directness over the presuppositionally weak features "plural" and "3rd person". We argue that this account both undergenerates and overgenerates. It cannot accommodate the typological asymmetries between 1st and 2nd person (e.g. the absence of speaker-inclusive 2PL), the role-specific use-conditions attached to forms like English Nurse We, the disappearance of honorific content under ellipsis, or the lexeme-specific contrasts seen, e.g., in Spanish nosotros vs. null pro. We propose a hybrid pragmatic-conventional alternative. Person and number are treated not as presuppositional heads but as components of complex anaphoric indices, with their semantic import encoded as constraints on admissible assignment functions. Assuming this system, we derive a markedness hierarchy 2 < 1 < 3 over indices defined by referential explicitness. A valence-neutral Taboo of Distance favors weak indices for the expression of social or psychological distance, while language-specific use-conditional constraints license particular weak indices in particular utterance contexts. Crucially, a conjunctive definition of semantic information over both truth-conditional and use-conditional dimensions allows weak indices enriched by conventional use-conditions to survive Quantity-based competition with their more explicit alternatives, dissolving the apparent conflict between informativity and indirectness. The result accommodates 1st person addresse honorifics, anti-honorific uses of the same features, and the existence of lexical idiosyncrasies in honorific inventories.

records.title: No country for old linguists: LLM–brain alignment underdetermines neural computation
records.abstract: Nastase et al. (2026) argue that large language models (LLMs) may illuminate language processing because both rely on distributed, context-sensitive representations shaped by statistical learning. Their rejection of simple cortical "boxology" is persuasive, and they articulate a strong case for the value of LLM-brain alignment research. The key question is what kind of inference LLM-brain alignment licenses. My claim here will be narrow: representational alignment can in principle constrain mechanistic hypotheses, but it does not by itself identify a mechanism. Nastase et al. acknowledge that an encoding model can capture features represented in neural activity without establishing a shared architecture or algorithm. Yet the authors sometime move from alignment to "shared computational principles" and ultimately to LLMs as mechanistic models of natural language. Indeed, their methodological caveat that alignment does not establish a shared architecture or algorithm sits uneasily with their conclusion that LLMs might instantiate the same computational principles as biological brains and provide a "fully mechanistic model" of language. I discuss what I consider to be problems of logical, causal, and computational underdetermination in Nastase et al.'s (2026) proposal.

records.title: Children's knowledge of negative free choice inferences
records.abstract: Sentences of the form ♢(A∨B), such as "Mia is allowed to buy the apple or the banana", give rise to a free choice inference (FCI), namely the inference that each disjunct is individually permitted, ♢A∧♢B. Previous studies have shown that children as young as five years of age compute such inferences. In this paper, we investigate negative free choice inferences (NFCIs). Sentences of the form ¬□(A∧B), such as "Mia doesn’t have to buy both the apple and the banana", give rise to the inference that each of the conjuncts is not required,¬□A∧¬□B. Adults reportedly derive such inferences less robustly than positive FCIs, a result that has been taken to support hybrid approaches on which positive FCIs are derived by a non-implicature mechanism, while NFCIs are genuine implicatures. Given children’s documented difficulties with scalar implicatures, this approach predicts that they will likewise have difficulty deriving NFCIs. We report two truth-value judgment experiments conducted with English-speaking adults and 5–7-year-old children, comparing positive and negative FCIs with positive and negative scalar implicatures. Experiment 1 tested modal statements; Experiment 2 extended the same contrasts to the nominal domain. In both experiments, children were largely adult-like with respect to positive FCIs. However, their behavior with NFCIs did not conform to the predictions of the hybrid approach. In the modal domain, children computed NFCIs nearly as often as positive FCIs, and more often than adults did; moreover, their performance on NFCIs matched their performance on negative SIs. In the nominal domain, however, this pattern disappeared: neither adults nor children computed NFCIs, and children’s performance on NFCIs no longer patterned with negative SIs. Although our findings replicate the polarity asymmetry previously observed in adults, we argue that the developmental data ultimately challenge the hybrid account of FCIs.

records.title: Rocks, Rabbits, and Computers: Large Language Models Do Not Adjudicate (Relevant Forms of) Nativism and Empiricism
records.abstract: The nativism and empiricism dispute in cognitive science turns on a disagreement about the domain-specificity or domain-generality of language’s biological basis. Biolinguists tend to adopt the former perspective, whereas competing approaches like usage-based approaches tend to adopt the latter. Where Large Language Models (LLMs) have been held up as theories or proxies for theories of human language acquisition or use, they have tended to be used in support of the view that these models provide an existence proof of natural language’s domain-general learnability. This paper reviews the dispute and argues that LLMs nevertheless fail to adjudicate nativism and empiricism. In short order, LLMs circumvent challenges relevant to language acquisition by human children in ways that reduce their significance to a theory of human language. These turn principally on an LLM’s relation to its environment during (pre- and post-) training, including the curation of domain-specific data on its behalf and its closure from extraneous environmental stimuli. It is argued that the hypothesis space that LLMs traverse during training is somewhat constrained by human engineers in virtue of this relation. In the same vein, it is argued that the Poverty of the Stimulus Argument to which LLMs are often aimed is not, in its form of most interest to linguists, an argument concerning the availability of data in the child’s environment, and the use of LLMs to this end miss the point.

records.title: The Name-Leash Hypothesis: Maternal Separation and the Origins of Displaced Reference
records.abstract: Displaced reference — the use of a signal for what is not in the perceptual field — is a defining feature of human language (Hockett 1960) and, as Bickerton (2009) argued, the central problem for any account of its origin. The standard scenario derives it from the need to recruit others to distant food; but where pointing, leading and pantomime would serve, an offline representational system is not obviously worth its cost. This paper proposes a different first case. In the cooperative-breeding arrangement reconstructed for early Homo (Hrdy 2009; Burkart et al. 2025), a mother handed her infant to an allomother and left to forage, so that mother and infant were repeatedly placed in perceptual situations that no longer specified one another. What is at issue is not distance but a partition between situations: how to go on holding one specific, non-fungible individual when one's own situation supplies no index of it. A perceptually grounded gesture has nothing to work on there; an individualized vocalization does. The first displaced signal, on this account, was a proper name rather than a food call. The semiotic core is the broken index. An index signifies through a connection that holds at the moment of signifying; when the referent goes, that connection lapses and cannot be restored by producing the signal again. What takes over its office is a sign of another type: a vocal form tied to one individual, which keeps the singularity of pointing while working without perceptual contiguity. Four stages that "proper name" otherwise runs together are separated — an infant-associated form, its displaced use by the mother alone, a mapping organized by the referent rather than by any caller, and a public name — with Kripkean rigid designation characterizing the last rather than the first. The token is relational at the outset, which makes the portable name the product of a first decomposition rather than an atom. On this reading the proper name is not a defective case within a system whose norm is the common noun, but the paradigm from which the principle of arbitrariness was tacitly generalized (Zimmerling 2025); and the relational handle the decomposition leaves behind is what seeds recombination. Evidence is drawn from cooperative breeding and life history, vocal-respiratory control, development, comparative vocal individuation in dolphins, chimpanzees and marmosets, and neural work on cross-modal identity representation. Three levels of decoupling are distinguished — from arousal, from here, and from now — and the mechanism is placed at the third, which the published comparative record does not document. The account is offered as a reconstruction, not a demonstration. This is version 4, revising version 3. The hypothesis is unchanged: §1.2 now states the mechanism in one pass, the four stages are separated, and the evidential status of each claim is marked. A companion Supplementary Materials document, not hosted here, develops the intellectual genealogy of the displacement problem, the pre-cooperative-breeding ecology, the modal philosophy of the sign, the synchronic windows on the genitive contour, and the cultural elaborations of the mechanism: doi:10.5281/zenodo.20488658.

records.title: When competing grammars fight it to a stalemate: The verbalization of the infinitive in Hungarian
records.abstract: In this paper, we analyze the appearance of the 1>2SG suffix on the infinitival paradigm in Modern Hungarian. This development is challenging for the existing accounts of verbal agreement in Hungarian because the 1>2SG suffix has originally been restricted to the finite paradigm. We argue that the full gamut empirical facts can be accounted for by recourse to three competing grammars for agreeing infinitives: N (where infinitivals are nominal), Vdeficient (where infinitivals are verbal, with a paradigm gap in cell 1>2SG) and V full (where infinitives are verbal, with no paradigm gap.) This results in there being two tribes of Modern Hungarian speakers: Tribe 1 (where N and Vdeficient compete very discreetly) and Tribe 2 (where Vfull is crowding N out). Grammar N is in line with É. Kiss’s (2002) proposal; whereas Grammars V can be plausibly modelled in moderately revised versions of Den Dikken’s (2004) and Bárány’s (2017) system (both of which were originally developed with the finite paradigm in mind). Finally, we argue that the failure of the innovative paradigm (Vfull) to spread fast and wide is due to three factors: (i) the relatively minor advantage offered by Vfull to its alternatives, (ii) the fact that infinitival agreement in general is fading in the language and (iii) the spread of the Balkan subjunctive, which provides a more established outlet for the verbalization of subordination.

records.title: Yes/no questions across Chinese varieties and English
records.abstract: This article provides a morphosyntactic and semantic analysis of nine yes/no question constructions across English and Chinese varieties (e.g., Mandarin, Yixing, Nanjing, Suzhou, Hefei, Kunming, Liangshan, many of which are understudied), and shows that the apparently complex crosslinguistic variation is in fact complete systematic variation generated by just three binary parameters. The first parameter is whether or not the question involves a polar Disjunction Phrase (DisjP) in syntax. The questions with a polar DisjP vary in two more parameters: whether there is overt or covert wh-movement, and whether the DisjP is realised as a single Vocabulary Item or multiple. Our study has two theoretical implications. The first is for question semantics and typology: we provide syntactic and morphological evidence for two types of interrogative C0s in Hamblin’s (1973) question semantics; we also argue that the yes-no questions without DisjP do not involve any wh-element, and thus no (c)overt wh-movement or even genuine wh-in-situ, thus enriching the typology of questions. Our second theoretical contribution lies in theories of parametric variation. The three parameters proposed in this article have three different sources, all of which should be taken into account in parametric theories: linearization, phonological realization of features during Lexical Insertion, and the (un)availability of features in the lexicon.

records.title: phonokit: a toolkit to create phonological representations in Typst
records.abstract: Creating high-quality phonological representations in academic documents is often time-consuming and requires juggling multiple tools and LaTeX packages (most notably TikZ). This vignette introduces phonokit, an open-source Typst package designed to streamline the creation of phonological structures while maintaining typographical precision. The package provides intuitive functions for IPA transcription (supporting tipa input conventions), IPA vowel charts and consonant tables with built-in language inventories and flexible arrows, prosodic representations (syllables, feet, prosodic words, metrical grids), sonority profiles, autosegmental phonology (feature spreading, tone, delinking), multi-tier representations for complex non-linear structures such as Government Phonology and CV phonology, feature geometry, SPE feature matrices, Optimality Theory tableaux, Harmonic Grammar, Noisy Harmonic Grammar, Maximum Entropy grammars, and Hasse diagrams for constraint rankings. All functions prioritize minimal input syntax while automatically handling complex typographical challenges such as dynamic spacing, line crossing prevention, and proper alignment. phonokit aims to reduce cognitive load in document preparation, allowing phonologists to focus on content rather than formatting. The package is freely available through Typst's package repository and is under active development.

records.title: Structurally prominent linguistic items hold a privileged state in working memory: Time-course evidence for rapid access
records.abstract: Real-time language processing relies on a capacity-limited working memory system to encode and maintain (extra-)linguistic information. Prior research shows that structural information is rapidly used to distinguish targets from distractors in memory access, but the exact mechanisms underpinning this remain unclear. Here we consider two hypotheses. One is that structurally prominent, target representations are actively maintained in a privileged, focal attentional state that allows rapid, direct access. Another possibility is that structural prominence serves as a retrieval cue to distinguish target representations stored in a passive, non-focal state. These hypotheses can be distinguished by determining the relative time course of memory access to targets vs. distractors. To do this, we conducted a secondary analysis of a published dataset that measured the looking behavior during the online resolution of the structurally constrained Turkish local reciprocal birbirleri in a visual world paradigm. Bayesian analyses on gaze proportions and new fixations show evidence for reliable and faster access to targets relative to distractors. We interpret this as evidence for a functional divide within linguistic memory that is shaped by hierarchical syntactic structure, whereby structurally prominent target items are held in a privileged focal state, while distractors that lack this privileged status are accessed via a slower retrieval mechanism.

records.title: English Quantified Partitives are derived by Extraposition plus NP-deletion
records.abstract: This squib argues that English ‘quantified partitives’ like some of the sheep are underlyingly some sheep of the sheep with the partitive-PP extraposed and the stranded NP sheep deleted. This theory unifies quantified partitives with bare quantifiers (quantifiers which can delete their NP-complements), explaining why exactly the same quantifiers are available in both. It also explains why only extraposable NP-modifiers are available in either construction. The NP-deletion theory avoids problems faced by previous theories, including those that posit silent nouns, like some UNIT of the sheep and ‘surface true’ theories, which posit neither silent elements nor deletion.

records.title: Dependent clauses in Albanian: A Balkan feature
records.abstract: Balkan languages are known for the use of the finite verb in control contexts, unlike Romance and Germanic languages. However, both Albanian and Aromanian varieties (Southern Albania) also present non-finite verbal forms in dependent clauses, in alternance with finite structures. Thus, Tosk/ standard Albanian shows both finite clauses in control contexts, and, in some contexts, a participial construction introduced by the prepositions për ‘for’, pa ‘without’, tu/ duke for the gerund. In Gheg variety all dependent contexts include an invariant form of the verbal base preceded by the preposition me ‘with’. Aromanian, like Tosk Albanian and Romanian, selects finite constructions in alternation with infinitives introduced by the preposition di ‘of’ or ti ‘for’. The article analyzes these data in keeping with recent papers by Chomsky which develop a Strong Minimalist approach to syntax.

records.title: Deriving clause incorporation in Inuktitut
records.abstract: While previous research on incorporation has mainly focused on how (typically uninflected) nouns come to be incorporated into verb complexes, it is less well known that some languages also permit the incorporation of complex verbal constituents (e.g. Pittman, 2009; Barrie and Mathieu, 2016; McKenzie, 2022). In this paper, I investigate a previously underdescribed construction in Inuktitut (Inuit-Yupik-Unangan), in which an embedded clause is morphologically incorporated into a higher affixal verb of possession 'have', creating an existential. The embedded nominal arguments are stranded and case marked like antipassive objects rather than with the expected ERG and ABS morphology. I argue that the incorporated element is a pseudorelative clause, a CP-sized predicate of a small clause related to its nominal subject by control (e.g. Cinque 1995), based on structural parallels with pseudorelatives found cross-linguistically. Clause incorporation as opposed to noun incorporation arises in Inuktitut because the incorporating verb takes the entire pseudorelative structure, rather than a nominal, as its complement; this, in turn, motivates a postsyntactic model of incorporation that requires the syntactic structure as its input (e.g. Compton and Pittman, 2010; Yuan, 2025). Additionally, the case patterns found in incorporated clauses reveal that both ERG and ABS case assignment are tied to the extended CP domain (e.g. Compton, 2018; Carrier, 2020; Yuan, 2022), and are not associated with lower clausal fields such as the vP and TP domains.

records.title: Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio: Quantifying the Dual-Track Mechanism of Gender Assignment in Latvian Loanwords
records.abstract: Existing research has repeatedly observed the tendency for English loanwords to cluster in the masculine gender across different recipient languages, yet the origin of this pattern remains difficult to determine, as fixed morphological rules and default assignments are frequently analysed together. This study proposes the Fixed Suffix Dependency Ratio (FSDR) to quantify the degree of reliance on fixed derivational suffixes across different genders, and to distinguish between morphological anchoring and free-choice in distribution. By examining 1,832 Latvian noun lemma types, the results reveal a significant FSDR asymmetry within the loanword system: feminine loanwords rely significantly more on fixed derivational suffixes, while masculine loanwords are more concentrated in the free-choice zone. This pattern exhibits loanword specificity and has become more pronounced in contemporary usage. FSDR therefore provides a quantitative framework for testing default gender and shows how masculine default can be activated and reinforced under language contact.

records.title: U comin’ or not? Systemic Erosion and Tense Loss in Singaporean English
records.abstract: Language is evolving, not only in vocabulary, but in grammar itself. This paper examines the long-term evolution of question structure in Singaporean SMS English. Using a diachronic corpus of approx. 56,000 English-dominant SMS messages sent in Singapore between 2003 and 2015. Through regex-based classification, we identify a sharp rise in reduced and elliptical question forms (e.g “U coming?”), coinciding with technological transitions in mobile messaging. Drawing on an affordance-based framework (Hutchby 2001; Norman 1999), we argue that interface features such as character limits, predictive text and autocorrect exert pragmatic pressures that favour brevity and omission. While early reductions reflect cost-saving measures under SMS constraints, these forms persist even after the introduction of unlimited texting, suggesting the sedimentation of interface-driven norms. We theorise these patterns as part of an “affordance-grammar” feedback loop, wherein technological affordances shape usage patterns that over time reconfigure grammatical norms. This study contributes to corpus-based pragmatics by illustrating how interface design can precipitate macro-level grammatical shifts in informal digital communication

records.title: A representationalist theory of the semantics of reciprocals
records.abstract: As has been noted in the literature, a reciprocal pronoun can have two or more separate antecedents simultaneously, as in "Tom shouted and Mary cried each other's names", contradicting all previous accounts of the syntax and semantics of reciprocals. This fact and some related observations are shown to motivate a representationalist theory of the syntax-semantics interface in which the semantic representation of each lexical item is a set of elementary predications and semantic composition is allowed to involve taking the union of such sets.

records.title: Tone diachrony beyond tonogenesis: Reconstructing the tone melodies of nouns in Proto-Edoid (Niger-Congo)
records.abstract: The immediate goal of this paper is to reconstruct nominal tone in the Edoid family using the comparative method, one branch within the Benue-Congo subfamily of the Niger-Congo phylum, a stock for which no original tonogenesis event is discernible. To this end, we develop the Proto-Edoid Tone (PEdT) database drawn from 40 sources on 21 modern Edoid languages, totaling over 3000 individual data points, from which 436 cognates can be identified. Based on the PEdT database, we systematically compare tone patterns across the four proposed branches of Edoid, which results in a number of tonal correspondences which we reconstruct as combinations of tone on a noun class prefix and tone on a nominal stem. We call these nominal tone melodies. Based on these intermediate reconstructions, we reconstruct tone in Proto-Edoid as a symmetrical set of melodies **L-L, **L-LH, **L-H, **L-HL, **H-L, **H-LH, **H-HL, and **H-H. From these Proto-Edoid melodies, we track several recurring tone changes, the most common of which are Rightward H-Shift (e.g. the Great Edo Tone Shift, *H-L > L-H), H-Obligatoriness (i.e. adding a H to all-L words), and H-Lowering (i.e. *H > ꜜH, M, or L). These tone changes show both the hallmarks of regular sound change as well as many unexpected reflexes which cannot be explained at this point, setting the stage for future work on Edoid tone and how it relates to Proto-Benue-Congo and ultimately Proto-Niger-Congo.

records.title: Natural class reasoning in segment deletion rules
records.abstract: Logical Phonology is characterized by an insistence on a rigorous definition of the natural classes defining rule targets and environments, and by three novel operators which replace the -> operator of classical generative phonology. Following these ideas to their logical conclusion has a counterintuitive consequence for the analysis of segment deletion rules: Delete The Rich: If some—but not all-X's delete in some phonological context Y__Z, the X's that delete must be more richly specified than those which do not. This prediction is illustrated using deletion processes in Hungarian and Turkish. In Hungarian, there is independent evidence for underlyingly distinct sources of h, and these two h's show differential behavior with respect to deletion. In Turkish, positing distinct sources for deleting and non-deleting k allows for a unified handling, within the narrow phonology, of apparent exceptions and an atypical form of non-derived environment blocking. Together, these two case studies show that Delete The Rich is not an empirical problem.

records.title: The Sound of Reference
records.abstract: Noam Chomsky and his colleagues have proposed that human languages are basically designed for construction of inner thoughts so that individual humans can plan ahead, thus giving selectional advantage to the species. The sound part of language in this view is ancillary, it is meant only for the externalization of thought. Call it a ‘thought-only’ view of language. We challenge this view by showing that the thought-only conception of language cannot accommodate the referential function of languages. We probe the issue with a focus on what philosophers call Singular Terms that enable a language-user to pick out, identify, and draw attention to an individual object. The presence of singular terms in a human language not only gives a shape to human thoughts about individuals, it ensures that such thoughts are shared between conspecifics. Since such sharing cannot be accomplished without explicit articulation, the sound of singular terms is essential for human language, it is not ‘ancillary.’

records.title: Concord is Insatiable Agree: Heterogeneous Case and Phi Patterns in Slavic and Finnic
records.abstract: This paper argues that nominal concord does not require dedicated feature-percolation mechanisms. Building on the interaction/satisfaction model of Agree and on the horizons-based theory of locality, it proposes that concord arises when an insatiable probe successively interacts with all accessible feature-bearing constituents in an extended nominal projection, transmitting case and phi features. The analysis naturally derives standard concord patterns and a typological asymmetry between case concord and phi concord. It is then applied to heterogeneous case patterns in Slavic numeral–noun constructions, where case stacking and a markedness-based rule for morphological realization account for the contrast between direct and oblique cases. The proposed account extends to Russian paucal constructions under both the “paucal case” hypothesis and the “paucal number” approach defended in the paper. Finally, Estonian pseudopartitives are shown to be compatible with the proposed approach to concord once the Estonian case hierarchy is independently recognized to be partially ordered, with genitive and partitive incomparable in markedness. The resulting account unifies a range of apparently highly idiosyncratic Slavic and Finnic concord phenomena using independently motivated theoretical mechanisms and refining some of these mechanisms in the process.

records.title: The shapes of meaning: Diagrams in lexical semantics
records.abstract: Diagrams in lexical semantics come in all shapes and sizes, but there is currently no good understanding of the design space that allows for this variety. This paper derives that space from the combination of a small number of graphic and semantic parameters, thereby contributing to our insight in this increasingly common visual metalanguage in linguistics and related disciplines concerned with meaning.

records.title: Intermediate steps of lowering in Tigrinya
records.abstract: This paper presents a pattern of complementizer displacement in the Ethio­Semitic language Tigrinya (Ethiopia, Eritrea) that argues for the existence of a morphosyntactic operation of lowering that may involve successive steps (Embick and Noyer 2001; Arregi and Pietraszko 2021). In Tigrinya, underlyingly clause­-final complementizers may displace leftward and downward throughout a head-final verb cluster. This displacement is associated with morphological consequences, in the form of stem allomorphy and the spreading of relative morphology. Importantly, these effects show up also in intermediate positions, on auxiliaries that are crossed by lowering. As a result, the morphosyntax of Tigrinya complementizers provides evidence for intermediate steps of lowering, and against proposals in which lowering effects do not involve the dislocation of a morpheme (e.g. Brody 2000; Adger et al. 2009; Platzack 2013; Svenonius 2016).

records.title: Agreement by proxy
records.abstract: Proposes some new uses for an old idea (Butt (1993, 1995), Bhatt (2005), Legate (2005), Baker and Willie (2010)): that if X Agrees with Y and Y Agrees with Z, X should be taken for all syntactic and morphological purposes to be in an Agree relation with Z. I refer to the relation between X and Z as 'agreement by proxy', and argue that recognizing agreement by proxy allows for very simple statements on the conditions on locality of Agree. The resulting theory derives a version of the ban on improper movement and on A-movement out of CPs, and predicts correctly that these bans can be circumvented under the right circumstances. It also derives a version of the notion of 'phase unlocking', and accounts for some facts about the interaction of long-distance movement with agreement in Passamaquoddy-Wolastoqey (Algonquian).

records.title: Context Shift and Viewpoint Shift: Super Monsters Revisited
records.abstract: While Kaplan's classic theory of indexicals took them to be rigidly anchored to the context of the actual speech act, more recent research has found multiple cases in which an indexical depends on the context of a reported speech act, suggesting that attitude verbs can sometimes shift the context (in Kaplan's terms, attitude operators can be "monsters"). It was further proposed that context shift is sometimes overtly realized in sign language by Role Shift, an operation in which the signer visibly adopts someone else's perspective. However, in ASL and LSF, Role Shift involves peculiarities that have motivated the development of non-standard context-shifting operators ('Super Monsters'), and also of alternative treatments (in terms of demonstrations). First, Role Shift arises not just in attitude reports but also in action reports, where no monsters have been found in spoken language. Second, Role Shift forces elements within its scope to be interpreted in a maximally iconic fashion ('Maximize Iconicity'), something that has not been found in spoken language monsters. We argue that a key observation, familiar from informal descriptions, has been missed by formal analyses: Role Shift usually shifts the viewpoint ('camera position') relative to which iconic elements are evaluated. Building on the formal framework of Iconological Semantics, which has an explicit pictorial component, we develop a minimal analysis in which Role Shift only involves overt viewpoint shift. We find that it arguably leaves some facts unaccounted for, and consider an alternative in which Role Shift involves both context shift and viewpoint shift, hence a new take on Super Monsters. While our main new data are from ASL, we include gestural examples that suggest that the analysis could be extended to speech with gestures.

records.title: Two types of exclusive doubling in Vietnamese
records.abstract: This study focuses on the syntax-semantic mismatches arising from the doubling of exclusive focus particles ‘only’ in Vietnamese: (i) adverbial chỉ with adfocal mỗi and with (ii) sentence-final particle (SFP) thôi . Despite multiple occurrences, only one particle is interpreted as the exclusive operator. Following the operator-particle approach, I propose that only adverbial chỉ is the operator, which establishes different syntactic dependencies with mỗi and thôi that are truth-conditionally void: (i) covert movement triggered by focus [FOC] features in adverbial-adfocal doubling, and (ii) syntactic Agree with exclusive [EXCL] features in adverbial-SFP doubling. The non-uniformity is supported by their distinct locality profiles and (non-)sensitivity to intervention by quantificational elements. Furthermore, I argue that focus and quantificational elements constitute different featural classes for minimality-based intervention.

records.title: The Mass-Count Distinction, Davidsonian Events and Other Non-Nominal Domains
records.abstract: Verbs in European languages do not come with a morphosyntactic mass-count distinction. Yet it has become standard to apply a semantic mass-count distinction to the verbal domain of events as well, taking the applicability of for- and in-adverbials to be indicative of a mass-count distinction in a broader sense. But the verbal domain of events in fact behaves like a classifier system, rather than dividing into mass and count. This can be accounted for on an emerging view of the mass-count distinction according to which countability is not an integral part of lexical meaning, but is ‘added on’ or ‘made available’, whether syntactically, semantically or both. The paper discusses a range of data, partly from German, that support such a grammar-based view of countability for verbs with respect to the event argument position as well as for other non-nominal domains. It also points out that the semantics of for-adverbials need not make recourse to a mass-count distinction if it is part of a broader phenomenon of part quantification (Moltmann 1991)

records.title: TAG is not a Construction Grammar, it is a Transformational Grammar, or is it? — A comment on the nature of grammatical relations
records.abstract: This paper discusses recent claims about Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG) being suited as the formalization for phrasal Construction Grammar approaches. It is shown that inheritance as such is not a sufficient means to establish relations between linguistic objects and to capture generalizations. Of course, TAG has all the technical tools that are needed for expressing the generalizations, but if they are used appropriately, TAG is more similar to a Transformational Grammar than to a Construction Grammar. This discussion helps to show where the shortcomings of phrasal Construction Grammar proposals are and what should be done instead if one wants to assume a constructionist approach.

records.title: Mood and Modality
records.abstract: This chapter is dedicated to the grammatical category of mood and its relation to modality. It overviews some key empirical phenomena discussed in the literature, such as existence of subjunctive clauses with distinct profiles (selected vs. optional vs. polarity subjunctives), possibility of mood marking in embedded vs. root clauses, as well as mood marking in other environments such as purpose and relative clauses. The chapter compares analyses of these phenomena under three main theoretical approaches, outlining their virtues as well as the challenges that they face: ordering source-based theories, which link the choice of mood to the presence of an ordering source in the semantics of a modal, commitment-based theories, which consider the choice of mood to depend on the truth of the embedded proposition in some dedicated set of possible worlds, and alternatives-based theories, for which mood reflects presence of obligatorily activated focus alternatives to the embedded proposition. The chapter also raises the question of what the contribution of mood morphology is, suggesting that the connection between the modal meanings and mood morphemes is indirect: mood morphemes are better viewed as exponents of agreement with higher modal-introducing elements rather than the source of modality.

records.title: A New Analysis of the Morphological Structure of Japanese Verbal Adjectives
records.abstract: The present paper reanalyses the morphosyntactic–semantic structure of Japanese verbal adjectives (VAs), also referred to as i-adjectives. Traditionally, inflected forms of this class, such as 'takaku' from 'takai' "be high/tall", have been analysed as consisting of the so-called stem 'taka-' and the so-called ending '-ku'. However, given multiple morphosyntactic and semantic parallelisms with verbal stems such as 'tabe' from 'taberu' "eat", it is more plausible that 'takaku' as a whole functions as the stem of the verbal adjective. This analysis thus analyses 'taka-' as one of the two immediate constituents of the VA stem 'takaku', which encodes, as a VA radical, the lexical meaning specific to the VA, and '-ku' as the other constituent, functioning as the VA thematic — namely, stem-forming — suffix, which licences the VA radical as a syntactic constituent of the VA category at the sentential level (from the perspective of DM '-ku' may be regarded as an overt instantiation of the categorial head a). The discussion then examines how VAs encode the tense value [−PAST], proposing an alternative interpretations: either the phonologically null inflexional suffix '-Ø', as in [[[taka]i]Ø], acquires the [−PAST] value through paradigmatic opposition to '-ta', specified as [+PAST], as in [[[taka]k+at]ta]; or, '-i', as in [[[taka]i], is an amalgam of the VA thematic suffix and the non-past tense suffix. On the other hand, the atemporal form 'takaku' lacks any temporal suffix, as in [[[taka]ku] ]. Based on this, the paper further examines the allomorphy of the VA thematic suffix: '-ku ≈ -i ≈ -(k)i ≈ -ke'. The study also examines the structural parallels between VAs and true verbs and the lack of surface-level parallelism between the negative forms of VAs and those of true verbs. Finally, it surveys syntactic and logical-propositional differences between verbal-adjectival and nominal-adjectival constructions.

records.title: Treatment of wh-expletives in Haryanvi
records.abstract: This paper examines long-distance wh-dependencies in Haryanvi, an Indo-Aryan language of northern India, and in particular the construction in which the element "ke" appears in the matrix clause while the interrogative phrase remains in situ in the embedded clause. Haryanvi patterns with Hindi-Urdu in allowing two strategies for forming a long-distance wh-dependency: the wh-phrase may move into the matrix clause, or it may stay in the subordinate clause, in which case "ke" surfaces preverbally in the matrix clause. Drawing on data elicited from native speakers, I establish that the Haryanvi construction obeys the generalisations that have been reported for Hindi-Urdu: the scope of any number of embedded wh-phrases can be extended, a scope marker and a true wh-phrase cannot occur in the same clause, a scope marker must appear in every intervening clause, and the matrix clause can contain neither the sentential expletive yo nor negation. Against this background I argue that "ke" is not a scope marker at all. It is a wh-expletive that questions the sentential expletive "yo," which is base-generated at the edge of the embedded CP and co-indexed with it. Both elements raise to the edge of the matrix vP, so that the surface order follows without the embedded wh-phrase taking matrix scope. The account therefore leaves the wh-in-situ character of Haryanvi and Hindi-Urdu intact. Keywords: wh-expletive, wh-scope marking, wh-in-situ, Haryanvi, Hindi-Urdu

records.title: The complementary-distribution challenge for phonological learning: The case of [h] and [ŋ] in English
records.abstract: The distribution of [h] and [ŋ] in English poses a well-known challenge for the structuralist assumption that segments in complementary distribution are allophones of the same phoneme. In this paper, we show that this distribution also poses a challenge within generative linguistics, a challenge of explanatory adequacy. The challenge is to explain why the English-learning child does not acquire a grammar in which [h] and [ŋ] are derived from the same underlying representation. The generative literature has not identified this as a problem, largely because of the assumption that [h] and [ŋ] are too phonetically dissimilar to participate in an alternation. However, we argue that phonetic accounts do not eliminate the challenge. We discuss simplicity-based theories of learning and show that under naive representational assumptions, simplicity-based learners prefer to derive [ŋ] from an underlying /h/, rather than a longer sequence of /ng/ (or an underlying /ŋ/), and therefore make wrong predictions about English speakers’ knowledge. The same learners, however, make correct predictions when combined with a representational framework that assumes underspecification and lexical redundancy rules. We therefore conclude that the acquisition problem can be addressed using simplicity-based learning, and that the complementary distribution of [h] and [ŋ] provides an argument for underspecification and lexical redundancy rules.

records.title: Form-meaning mismatches in Nanosyntax
records.abstract: This study reflects on my work between 2013 (PhD) and 2023 through the lens of form-meaning mismatches. It discusses cases of syncretism and fusion, doubling and multiple exponence, as well as zero-to-one and one-to-zero mismatches, drawing on data from degree morphology, negation and derivational morphology. I show how two central tools of Nanosyntax (Starke 2009, Caha 2009), namely decomposition into syntactico-semantic features and phrasal lexicalisation, allow to account for these phenomena. The study argues that form-meaning mismatches do not require exceptional mechanisms, but follow naturally from the way hierarchically organised feature structures are packaged and stored as lexical items. The same architecture underlies cases in which form and meaning appear to correspond one-to-one. Form-meaning mismatches are nevertheless particularly revealing, as they provide a clear window onto the underlying structure of language.

records.title: Grammar across perceptual dimensions
records.abstract: Some grammatical properties are extremely stable across sign languages, and may arise spontaneously in homesign systems. In particular, signers refer to objects and individuals by creating locations for them in signing space, and sometimes by turning or rotating to these locations to adopt their perspectives. Both the stability and spontaneous emergence of this location-based system suggest that it might be rooted in knowledge that is core to human cognition. We show that non-signers are sensitive to non-trivial constraints on these referential locations when they are realized in gestures (Study 1, two experiments), but also when they are realized using non-gestural means, including color, shape, position, and even sound (Study 2, four experiments). The findings suggest that the sophisticated location-based referential system of sign languages might have a broader cognitive source that is not specific to the visual modality. The fact that non-signers show sensitivity to such constraints across a variety of modalities moreover suggests that even if these general biases can be grammaticalized (as they have been in sign languages), they do not have to be (as evidenced by the absence of sound-based loci in spoken languages).

records.title: Was magnitude estimation necessary? A secondary-data reassessment of Bard, Robertson, and Sorace (1996)
records.abstract: Was magnitude estimation necessary to establish acceptability judgments as serious linguistic measurements? I separate Bard, Robertson, and Sorace's broader case for graded acceptability from the narrower claim that magnitude estimation improves on simpler formal tasks. Using public method-comparison data from Sprouse, Schütze, and Almeida (2013) and Sprouse and Almeida (2017), I compare magnitude estimation with Likert, forced-choice, and yes/no judgments. The primary analysis follows a charter fixed before outcome analysis. I find a strong common item-level signal and the bounded Likert curvature that motivates magnitude estimation, but no systematic practical advantage unique to magnitude estimation in endpoint, prediction, or decision diagnostics. A post-outcome multiverse of 162 specifications confirms the result. Four 2017 rank-based forced-choice models show small incremental predictive gains, but these don't generalize to raw-scale models, yes/no judgments, or the 2013 data. The results preserve Bard et al.'s broader contribution (i.e., the formal measurement of graded acceptability) while weakening the case that magnitude estimation has a general practical advantage for the contrasts examined.

records.title: Tutrugbu Partial ATR (Dis)harmony in Search
records.abstract: Search, identifying the presence of a given configuration, can indirectly check if a string-peripheral segment is of a particular type: when, say, every high vowel from itself looks for the first vowel to its left, only the string-first high vowel, if there exists one, cannot find a preceding vowel. With this property, an analysis is proposed for the otherwise systematic ATR harmony between prefixes and a stem in Tutrugbu. The proposed analysis then gets adapted to incorporate the round harmony among some prefixes in the same language.

records.title: Willams Cycle effects and successive cyclicity unified
records.abstract: The Williams Cycle (Williams 2003) generalizes the correlation between a clause’s relative size and its selective opacity. Most previous accounts (Keine 2020, Poole 2022; Meadows 2023) maintain Phase Theory (Chomsky 2001) to explain reflexes of successive cyclicity, and propose an independent mechanism to derive Williams Cycle effects. I propose a unified analysis of Williams Cycle effects and successive cyclicity.Under my unified constraint, probing must proceed along well-formed functional sequence fragments. When cross-clausal subextraction proceeds successive cyclically, Williams Cycle effects are obviated. When successive cyclicity is unavailable, the clause’s movement to an equal-sized matrix projection feeds subextraction, but subextraction obeys the Williams Cycle.

records.title: Who invokes silent negation? The view from a hybrid negative concord language
records.abstract: Zeijlstra (2004, 2022) proposes an agreement-style grammar, where negative concord items (NCI) are existentials that must be licensed by a pronounced or silent negation. The silent negations are invoked by NCIs themselves and, in strict-NC systems, by the overt but meaningless negative marker (NM). This paper addresses two main issues. First, why is NM obligatory in strict systems, if NCIs can invoke silent negation? Second, is it possible for strict and non-strict NC to co-exist in a language, if the NM is meaningless in the first and meaningfully negative in the second case? The paper focuses on Hungarian, based on but going beyond existing literature (Surányi 2006; Kenesei 2009; É. Kiss 2015; Szabolcsi 2018a,b, and others). It combines Zeijlstra’s analysis for strict-NC with Chierchia’s (2013) analysis for non-strict NC. Hungarian is particularly interesting, because it is a hybrid, and so it requires accounts of the two kinds of NC that are compatible.

records.title: Linguistic and Social Aspects of Sibilant Palatalization in Homeland and Heritage Cantonese
records.abstract: This paper investigates the linguistic and sociocultural factors that influence sibilant palatalization among Cantonese speakers from two different speech communities, namely Hong Kong (homeland) and Toronto (heritage). We analyzed naturalistic speech data of 36 speakers from the HLVC corpus, including homeland (Gen-0) speakers from Hong Kong, as well as first- (Gen-1) and second-generation (Gen-2) immigrants from Toronto. Our findings highlight that linguistic factors including vowel roundedness, vowel height, and sibilant type (fricative vs. affricate) significantly impact palatalization patterns. Generation emerged as an important sociocultural factor, with Gen-2 speakers producing a higher ratio of palatalization and widening its phonological context. Ethnic identity and language use are further found to influence palatalization patterns within the heritage community. Overall, there is evidence showing that the two speech communities are at different stages of the sound change, and that the contact with English might be contributing to such difference.

records.title: West Circassian lessons on Phase Theory
records.abstract: This paper explores the connection between the opacity of phases and their status as spellout domains. Based on evidence from West Circassian, I argue that while a subset of phases are salient prosodic domains, syntactic opacity is not a consequence of transfer to PF, but of standard conditions on locality. Furthermore, the relation between phasehood and prosodic constituency holds only partially: some phases are not salient prosodic domains. West Circassian provides a compelling illustration of this mismatch due its polysynthetic profile. On the one hand, a complex syntactic constituent is identifiable as a prosodic domain due to being pronounced as a single prosodic word. On the other, the connection between syntactic opacity and locality constraints is demonstrated by dynamic phasehood which is connected to the licensing of polysynthetic phi-agreement.

records.title: Composure and composition
records.abstract: In this paper, I explore the distinction between non-truth-conditional affective a.k.a. expressive meanings (as in 'my fucking dog') and truth-conditional affective and affect-related meanings (as in 'my lovely/disgusting dog') from an architectural perspective. Specifically, I focus on the differences in whether and how these meanings interact semantically with their surroundings and discuss the implications of these differences for our formal theories of meaning. In particular, I show that expressive meanings do not have to interact semantically with their syntactic surroundings, but truth-conditional meanings do even when they are affect-related and not-at-issue. This contrast holds even when the two types of meaning are contributed by uncontroversially the same type of morphosyntactic objects, as is the case for affection-expressing diminutive suffixes (non-truth-conditional) vs. derogatory/pejorative suffixes (truth-conditional) in Russian. This warrants a complete separation of the two types of meaning in our formal semantic theories---contrary to theories that treat expressive meaning as some type or other of truth-conditional, but not-at-issue meaning. In addition, I demonstrate that we observe some of the same typology of affective and affect-related meanings as conveyed through "secondary" channels, such as prosody, facial expressions, and non-face gesture, as we do for fully conventionalized segmental morphemes (i.e., "words"). I furthermore show that we routinely make use of a productive mechanism of going from performative, non-truth-conditional expression of affect to demonstrations of such expression within pieces of truth-conditional meaning of the general form '(such that) it would make me/one go "DEMONSTRATION"', which we can then compose with other truth-conditional content. Once again, we observe this process at work both for "words" (e.g., in at least some instances of spoken word expressives used for degree intensification) and for other types of meaning--form mappings (e.g., facial expressions and/or prosody conveying some form of surprise-related or negative affect)---and we can, thus, apply the same formal analysis to all these cases. I take the cross-channel similarities in how the expressive vs. truth-conditional distinction manifests to be an argument against the common tendency to indiscriminately label any instances of affect-related meaning conveyed through "secondary" channels as "paralinguistic" and, thus, something that we as formal linguists should not concern ourselves with. [Note: While the July 2021 and subsequent versions of the paper relies on some of the same data as the January 2020 manuscript, it has been written entirely from scratch, with a new framing, proposal, and structure. The September 2026 version is a preprint, which is scheduled to appear in the special issue '(Not-)At-Issueness' of 'Languages', potentially with minor copyediting changes.]

records.title: Northern Toussian
records.abstract: Northern Toussian (ISO: tsp; Glottocode: nort2787) is a minority Niger-Congo lan- guage spoken in southwest Burkina Faso by the Toussian people. The Toussian languages are of uncertain genetic affiliation—they were originally classified as Gur (Mabia) languages, but the classification of the family has been disputed (Prost 1964, Naden 1989, Miehe 2012, Güldemann 2018). While there is adequate evidence to consider the Toussian languages to be Niger Congo, there has not been sufficient research to confidently assign it to a particular branch of the Niger-Congo family tree. This is much the same situation of the other so-called “peripheral Gur” languages like the Senoufo, Tiéfo, and Samu families, as well as the language Viemo. More precise classification of these languages not only requires historical linguistic work on Gur and each of these groups individually, but also consideration of the relationship of certain members of the Adamawa family, some of which have been shown to share many features in common with Gur languages (Kleinewillinghöfer 1996).
